Two Specialist Agents, One Incident: What an A2A Handoff Takes

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 21 min read (4276 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~21 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, A Kubernetes expert and an AWS expert worked the same failure over A2A.
  • Two in the morning, a checkout service starts failing, and two different agents can each see part of why.
  • It has been revealed that one is watching the cluster.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Originally published on data-agent.co.

In a recent development, A Kubernetes expert and an AWS expert worked the same failure over A2A. These are field notes on what the protocol handled, what it could not express, and what we had to build in between, measured over 63 runs against the real agent, on a real account, against real faults.

Two in the morning, a checkout service starts failing, and two different agents can each see part of why.

It has been revealed that one is watching the cluster. Within seconds it has the restart loop, the error, the deployment that went out on Tuesday, and the fact that this workload talks to something called payments-db. The other can read the inside of payments-db: the connection ceiling, the engine log, the parameter somebody changed last week.

Neither can finish the job alone. That is not a gap in the tooling that will close next year. It is what a modern incident actually looks like, and it is the reason we spent this quarter building a handover rather than a bigger agent.

Our agent's reads stop at the cluster boundary, on purpose. We read Kubernetes and the cloud control plane in place, which is what makes detection continuous and cheap rather than alarm-driven and expensive. The cost of that choice is that a managed database is a closed box, with its own telemetry, its own permissions and its own console.

A large share of what actually breaks a Kubernetes application is not in the cluster. It is the managed database behind it, the queue in front of it, the permission path, the security group. The agent watching the cluster can tell you which door the problem went through. It cannot follow it inside.

The instinct is to fix this by building one agent that sees everything. We think that instinct is wrong. Depth in a managed database means performance insights, engine logs and parameter history, with the permissions and domain knowledge that implies. Depth in Kubernetes means a live model of workloads, topology and drift. Build both into one agent and you get an agent that is mediocre at each, while you spend your quarters reimplementing somebody else's specialty.

The other option is the one every engineering organization already uses for humans. You keep a specialist, and you get good at the handover.

It is worth being concrete about what each side is actually for, because the moment people hear two agents they assume a competition.

Industry observers note that ours is DataAgent, an autonomous observability and remediation platform. It does three things, and it is worth naming them separately because the third one surprises people.

It has been revealed that it covers both layers. Kubernetes infrastructure and the application stack running on it, which matters because real incidents are rarely cleanly one or the other. A pod in CrashLoopBackOff because a connection pool is exhausted is an application fault wearing an infrastructure symptom, and an agent that sees only one layer describes half of it.

According to recent reports, it fixes, rather than reports, once you enable it for that fault class. The output is a gated change, not a document, and the latency follows from that: seconds to a first opinion, minutes to an approved action, because a fix that arrives after the incident is over is not a fix.

In a recent development, it right-sizes observability spend instead of adding to it. This one follows directly from reading in place. Detection never requires shipping telemetry into a store you pay for by the gigabyte, so continuously watching every pod and workload can reduce what you spend on observability rather than add to it. Most things you bolt onto a stack increase what you pay to collect. This one can reduce it, because an agent that proves which evidence each class of fault actually needs also knows what you never needed to ship, keep or index. That argument is the other half of why an agent that reads in place is worth building.

Industry observers note that the AWS DevOps Agent, which went generally available on 31 March 2026, researches in depth. Point it at a problem and it runs an autonomous, multi-step investigation without a prompt per step; in our runs, that took five to twelve minutes. Ask it a direct question instead and it answers in seconds. It reads what we cannot, and it is good at it, as far as the permissions you grant its Agent Space allow. It ends with an answer, evidence and recommendations.

Figure 1: Two agents at opposite ends of every axis that matters. That is what makes the handover worth building rather than an obvious feature bolt-on.

According to recent reports, line the two up and they sit at opposite ends of all five axes. Wide against deep. Cloud agnostic against AWS native. Seconds against minutes. A gated change against a researched answer. An agent that can reduce what you spend on watching, against one that bills for the watching it does.

It has been revealed that when two systems sit at opposite ends of every axis, the interesting engineering is not in either one. It is in the handover. The question is never which agent. It is when to hand over, what to send with it, and who owns the fix afterwards.

The two protocols in play here are not interchangeable, and the difference matters more than it first appears.

Industry observers note that MCP connects an agent to tools. You call, it returns, you continue. A2A connects an agent to another agent: you hand over a task, the other side works for minutes with its own initiative and its own sub-agents, and you follow it to a terminal state. A tool call has a result. A delegated task has a duration, a cost and an owner.

It has been revealed that A2A, hosted by the Linux Foundation since June 2025, reached version 1.0 in March 2026. A year after launch it had more than 150 supporting organizations, with integrations in Azure AI Foundry, Copilot Studio and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. It gave us the right abstraction. Discovery through Agent Cards, which v1.0 lets a publisher sign. Delegation as a task rather than a call. An eight-state lifecycle covering submitted, working, input required, auth required, completed, failed, canceled and rejected, which is exactly the vocabulary you need when the other side might come back asking for permission instead of an answer. Streaming progress, so a twelve-minute investigation is observable while it runs.

Industry observers note that in practice, two of those did less than the spec suggests. We never saw a signed card from AWS, and the agent never asked us for input: when it tried, its own ask-the-user step failed and it ended the turn.

Industry observers note that then the part nobody warns you about. A2A can express that a task was delegated. It cannot express who authorized it, who pays for it, or who to ask about it six weeks later.

We are not the only ones to notice a gap at this layer. Kang and Diponegoro audited MCP, A2A, ACP and two other protocols against six governance dimensions, including human escalation and audit and replay, and found that none of them covers the full set. Their conclusion is that governance is a missing layer above these standards. Ours is a narrower, operational version of the same finding: cost, authority and the identity of the requesting human are not in the protocol, so we built them outside it.

So the honest shape of this integration is that the protocol handled the conversation, and we built the layer around it.

That layer is eight steps, and only one of them is the actual delegation.

According to recent reports, figure 2: The handover, end to end. The protocol covers submit and follow. Everything that decides whether they happen, and what happens to the answer, is yours to build.

Coverage asks whether anything actually leaves this cluster. Preflight does a few cheap reads against whatever coverage found, and either rules it out or adds what it learned.

Then the brief, which is the step that decides the quality of everything downstream.

It has been revealed that A DataAgent incident already knows which dependencies leave the cluster, which ones our own reads have settled, and what the remaining question is. Sending that, rather than a bare question, is what makes minutes of someone else's research worth having. We measured the difference. Handed just the question, the specialist came back with two rows of evidence. Handed what we already knew and what we had already ruled out, it came back with four, in the same twelve minutes.

Recent findings suggest that context does not make the specialist faster. It moves its effort out of rediscovering what you already knew and into the part you actually needed.

Then the answer comes back, and you have a newly introduced problem: two analyses of one incident, written by two systems, with no guarantee they agree.

According to recent reports, so the handover ends in a reconciliation rather than an answer. Every finding lands in one of three buckets: it agrees with what we found, it adds something we did not have, or it conflicts with it. That last bucket is the valuable one, and it is exactly what nobody builds while they are still excited about the integration.

Industry observers note that the answer is evidence, not a verdict. It attaches to the incident, our own enrichment runs over it, and the blueprint that comes out the other side is still ours and still gated. The specialist stops at a recommendation, which is the right place for it to stop. Somebody still has to own the change, verify the system recovered, and carry the consequence if it did not.

None of the above is a cost story, but the moment a specialist bills by the second, economics becomes a design input whether you wanted it or not.

Put the two halves side by side and the shape is unusual. The detection layer that decides when to delegate adds nothing to the bill, because it reads in place, and it can right-size what you were already spending on observability. The depth layer, when we call it, is billed by the second at \$0.0083. So the money in this system is concentrated exactly where the judgment is: in deciding whether a question is worth asking a specialist at all. Here is what that looked like when we measured it.

Figure 3: Four runs against the same agent at the same rate. What changed was the brief, and whether we sent one at all.

Two findings, and only one of them is intuitive.

The informed brief cost two cents less than the plain one and returned twice the evidence. The agent fills whatever budget it is given, so context buys quality rather than savings. Do not let anyone sell an informed handover as a cost reduction, because the first invoice will contradict them.

A later run against the same fault added a caution. It found the real connection ceiling sat near 450, which contradicted the informed run's headline claim that the pool was stuck at a 130 cap. Four rows was more evidence, not more truth. Count the rows that are new, and check them.

Preflight checked a flagged database, found its connection count had never risen above zero, and ruled it out in two and a half seconds without opening a task. Disqualification is the only step in the whole system that removes money from the bill. Everything else moves cost around or improves what you get for it.

Recent findings suggest that every way to start a billed run passes a gate that shows the estimate first, because a cancelled run still bills for the seconds it consumed and stopping is therefore not a refund. And the requesting human's identity travels in the task metadata, so the audit trail names a person rather than a service account. Delegation splits authorization from accountability, and you have to put them back together yourself. And treat any estimate as a floor, not a quote: our buttons said about \$0.10 for a direct question and about \$3 for an investigation, and real runs cost up to \$0.80 and \$6.40.

Sources indicate that we have kept running the integration against the real agent since we first wrote this: 12 investigations and 51 direct questions so far. Some of what we learned changed the design. Some of it changed what we would tell you to expect.

Recent findings suggest that A2A gives you two ways to ask. A single streamed message, with no task behind it, answered a question in 10.6 seconds for about nine cents. The same question as a persistent task took 153.6 seconds and cost about \$1.28, because the task path reports back in batches 30 to 90 seconds apart. So we now split by question. A direct question streams. An investigation keeps the task, because the task is what gives you cancel, deduplication and a link back into the AWS console. One bill question went from almost five minutes and \$2.46 to 11 seconds and nine cents.

Industry observers note that figure 4: Two depths, priced on the button. A direct question streams back in under a minute; an investigation takes minutes. Nothing starts until somebody picks one, and declining costs nothing.

After the agent finished, our client kept the connection open for another three and a half to four minutes, and agent time bills by the second. A 20-second check fixed it: one run dropped from \$3.30 to \$2.78. If a specialist bills by the second, audit the seconds you add.

In a recent development, the specialist reads what its Agent Space is allowed to read. Without Performance Insights and the key to decrypt it, the inside-the-database answer was a permission dead end, after a 12-minute run that cost \$6.40. Without Cost Explorer access it could not answer a bill question at all. The good news is that one Agent Space can read a second AWS account as a secondary source, so the same chat answered a bill question in 24 seconds and an RDS question in 33.

According to recent reports, figure 5: One Agent Space, two AWS accounts: a primary source and a secondary one, both valid. Account numbers masked.

It has been revealed that asked for the current bill three times in seven minutes, it gave three totals up to 40 percent apart, and once reported zero usage where credits had cancelled the usage out. Asking for a table, the bottom line first, and gross figures before credits fixed the zero and matched Cost Explorer. Specify the shape of the answer, and show a person the variance rather than hiding it.

Industry observers note that figure 6: A direct question, answered as a table in under a minute. Read the last paragraph: the specialist leaves the fix to the plan it knows someone else owns.

Industry observers note that A brief of 10,681 bytes was rejected with an HTTP 500 validation error; collapsing repeated events brought it to 3,040 bytes and the run completed. Reading the Agent Card proves nothing about permission: it loads for any AWS login, including one that is refused on send, so we prove signing with a real five-cent question. A follow-up question does not carry its context over. And progress arrives in structured data parts that a text-only client drops, which left our panel silent for half a minute at a time.

An external agent is an escalation, never a tool inside our own root-cause analysis. It takes minutes where we take seconds. It would bill on every incident instead of only where coverage finds a real gap. Its text would flow straight into our conclusions. And its answers vary in ways a person should see. So it is offered, priced and confirmed, and what it says comes back as evidence, never as our verdict.

It has been revealed that everything above is architecture. Here is the same thing as a sequence of screens, captured against a running stack rather than mocked up. The AWS account number is masked; nothing else is retouched.

In a recent development, on the left, our own analysis: orders-api in CrashLoopBackOff, the PostgreSQL database out of connection slots, the rollout that did it thirteen minutes earlier. On the right, what our agent knows about the boundary: two dependencies leave the cluster, and it can name them.

Sources indicate that figure 7: One incident, both agents. The cluster-side analysis is already written and cost nothing. The panel on the right shows what our agent knows about the boundary, and the handoff already made for this incident.

Sources indicate that the agent is explicit about the line it cannot cross. It lists what it can read itself, the CloudWatch metrics, the RDS events, the parameter group, the security groups, and then what it cannot: performance insights, top SQL, engine log contents. That list is the argument for delegating, written by the agent that would otherwise be guessing.

Coverage, the dependencies, the brief mode it intends to send, and the price of asking, all on one line before any commitment exists.

Industry observers note that figure 8: Coverage, brief and price, visible before a decision. The running total against the monthly cap is there too, before the AWS invoice notes it.

Recent findings suggest that A slash in the ordinary chat composer offers the handoff alongside everything else. No separate console, no incantation to memorize.

Figure 9: The handoff is offered where the conversation already happens.

Recent findings suggest that the question is held, not sent. The estimate sits on the button itself, declining costs nothing, and pressing Enter again does not confirm.

Figure 10: The ask is held until somebody agrees to the spend. This is the only moment money can start, and it is a deliberate second action.

Recent findings suggest that since these screens were captured, the gate has changed shape. The single estimate became two priced choices, a direct question or an investigation, shown in Figure 4 above.

When the specialist finishes, its findings do not sit in a separate tool. They attach to the incident, post into its chat attributed to the agent that produced them, trigger our own enrichment over the new evidence, and record a verdict on that dependency so the next incident on it starts from what we learned.

It has been revealed that figure 11: Promotion, in four steps. The external answer becomes evidence on an incident we still own, and the edge verdict means the same question is not paid for twice.

Note the last line of that panel. The verdict was inconclusive, which settles nothing, so the dependency stays eligible for a future handover. A system that records only its successes would have quietly closed that door.

This is worth splitting honestly, because both sides get something they could not build alone.

Recent findings suggest that four things change. A different population of incidents reaches it: on its own it investigates what somebody already pointed it at, while continuous cluster-level detection also starts on the first-time fault nobody wrote a rule for. It arrives aimed, at the dependencies that actually left the cluster, with everything already settled marked as settled. Its answer gets reconciled rather than filed. And it gains a path to a gated fix.

It has been revealed that on our side, we get AWS depth we cannot reproduce and should not try to, an autonomous investigation that runs for minutes without supervision, and coverage in accounts where we would otherwise have no evidence at all. The findings feed our own enrichment, so the analysis and the plan stay ours.

Industry observers note that there is a cost on your side too, and it is worth naming. You stop starting every investigation by hand, which means the system needs to check for a running task before opening a duplicate, and it needs to carry your identity so the spend is attributable later. Both are work. Neither is optional.

The position, stated plainly: this runs your agent, in your Agent Space, on your bill. It is not a replacement for anything you have already chosen. It is what happens when continuous detection decides when to call it, what to send with the question, and what to do with the answer.

In a recent development, the checkout service is still failing at two in the morning, and neither agent can finish the job alone. One knows the cluster and can act on it. One knows the database and can explain it.

According to recent reports, the interesting work was never inside either of them. It was in deciding what to send, what to do with what came back, and who was accountable when it did.

Recent findings suggest that AWS is the first specialist, not the design. Google ships Gemini Cloud Assist investigations and Microsoft ships the Azure SRE Agent, each deep inside its own cloud and blind outside it. Our first attempt with Google's agent, on our own GKE cluster, is a fair preview of the work ahead: it answered in its own console, but refused every programmatic call, a block we have raised with Google. Multi-cloud is turning into multi-agent, and the handover layer is the part that spans it. That is the subject of our next post.

If you are wiring agents to agents yourself and have measurements of your own, we would like to compare notes.

Industry observers note that at the list price of \$0.0083 per agent-second, twelve minutes (720 seconds) comes to about \$5.98. Idle time is not billed, but a cancelled run still bills for the seconds it already used. Treat any estimate as a floor: in our runs, an investigation estimated at about \$3 cost up to \$6.40. Put the estimate in front of whoever approves the run, not after it.

New AWS customers get a two-month AWS DevOps Agent trial. Each trial month includes up to 20 hours of investigations. That is enough to measure brief quality and preflight hit rate before list pricing applies.

All eight, but two are easy to miss: input required and auth required. Both mean the remote agent has paused and is waiting on you. Treat them as a question to route to a human or a policy, not as a failure. Treat completed, failed, canceled and rejected as terminal.

A2A v1.0 lets an Agent Card carry a JWS signature computed over a canonical form of the card, but signing is optional, and in our runs the AWS DevOps Agent never presented a signed card. A readable card does not prove you are allowed to send either: AWS's card loads for any AWS login, including one that is refused on send. Check the signature where one exists, and prove permission with a small real request before you send incident context.

Use MCP when you want a tool: you call it, it returns, you continue. Use A2A when the other side prepares its own work, runs for minutes and may ask you for input or permission along the way. If the work has a duration, a cost and an owner, it is a task, and A2A models it better.

In a recent development, in the setup described here, the integration point is the incident itself. The cluster-side agent's live model of workloads and dependencies tells it which dependencies leave the cluster, and it hands those questions to a specialist agent over A2A as a task, with a brief of what is already known. The specialist's findings come back as evidence: they attach to the incident, post into its chat attributed to the agent that produced them, and record a verdict on that dependency. The remediation plan stays gated and owned by whoever owns the incident.

The specialist. AWS DevOps Agent reached general availability on 31 March 2026 (AWS What's New, InfoQ). It is priced at \$0.0083 per agent-second, with no charge for idle time (AWS pricing).

In a recent development, the protocol, and its gaps. Richard Kang and Yudho Diponegoro, "Governance Gaps in Agent Interoperability Protocols: What MCP, A2A, and ACP Cannot Express" (arXiv).

The Linux Foundation has hosted the Agent2Agent protocol since June 2025 (Linux Foundation). Its first stable version, v1.0, shipped in March 2026 (Google Open Source Blog). The v1.0 changes, task states and Agent Card signing are listed in the A2A docs.

At the one-year mark, more than 150 organizations supported A2A, with integrations in Azure AI Foundry, Copilot Studio and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime (Linux Foundation).

Other clouds, other specialists. Microsoft, Azure SRE Agent documentation (Microsoft Learn). Google Cloud, Gemini Cloud Assist investigations (Google Cloud docs).

According to recent reports, going deeper. If you are building the same kind of loop, the detect, diagnose, act and verify cycle is walked end to end in our free, open-source autonomous SRE training series. For the cost side of reading in place, see Precision vs. Recall: Why Observability Costs So Much.

Sources indicate that our figures. Run times, costs and evidence counts are our own measurements against the AWS DevOps Agent at list price, in our own AWS account, against real faults. They are not a customer's bill and not a vendor benchmark. Dollar figures are measured wall time multiplied by the published rate, not an AWS invoice. Runs before 29 September include up to four minutes our own client spent waiting after the agent had finished, since fixed; the runs in Figure 3 predate that fix.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that azure kills your o3 22 days before OpenAI does.
    • Industry observers note that most people track the model maker's deprecation page.
    • A second trap: on Azure, your code calls a deployment name you chose, not the model ID.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that azure kills your o3 22 days before OpenAI does. Not December. Same model, two dates:.

    Also retiring on Azure on November 19:.

    Industry observers note that most people track the model maker's deprecation page. But the cloud that hosts the model keeps its own calendar, with its own dates and its own replacements. Azure does, Amazon Bedrock does, Google Vertex AI does. Sometimes the cloud is later. This time it's three weeks earlier.

    A second trap: on Azure, your code calls a deployment name you chose, not the model ID. Grepping for o3 finds nothing if your deployment is called reasoning-prod.

    List every deployment with its model and version:.

    Then compare each model and version with Azure's model retirement page, not OpenAI's.

    Industry observers note that A model inventory that says "o3" isn't enough. It needs "o3, version 2025-04-16, on Azure, deployment reasoning-prod". The host decides the date.

    Versyka's retirement calendar keeps cloud dates separate from the maker's (Azure, Bedrock and Vertex AI each get their own), so a model on Azure is checked against Azure's date.

    Where do your models run: the maker's API, or a cloud?

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, before work starts, your contract should fix five things above all: what will be delivered, how each milestone is accepted, when payments are due, that all intellectual property transfers to you on payment, and how either side can exit.
    • A game design document or a short development brief can serve as the attachment.
    • Each milestone should produce something you can run, with criteria a third person could check.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, before work starts, your contract should fix five things above all: what will be delivered, how each milestone is accepted, when payments are due, that all intellectual property transfers to you on payment, and how either side can exit. Everything else supports those five. Have a lawyer review the final document. This checklist helps you arrive with the right questions.

    A game design document or a short development brief can serve as the attachment.

    Each milestone should produce something you can run, with criteria a third person could check.

    Sources indicate that the review period protects both sides. Slow feedback is the most common cause of late projects.

    For the choice of pricing model, see fixed price vs time and materials.

    Our guide to version control for game teams explains how to set this up.

    It has been revealed that ask for a list of every asset, plugin, font, sound and library that is not original, with its licence. Marketplace assets usually allow commercial use within a game but not resale. Some open-source licences place conditions on distribution. You need to know before launch, not after a complaint.

    A non-disclosure agreement should be signed before you share the design. It should cover the idea, documents, builds and business information, for a stated period, with standard exceptions for information that is already public.

    It has been revealed that games change during development. The contract should say how: a written change request, an estimate of cost and time, and approval before work begins. A small pre-agreed change budget makes this faster.

    An exit clause that works is the best protection against a partnership that stops working. See why outsourcing partnerships fail.

    It has been revealed that if the game collects personal data, serves children or runs in regulated markets, name who is responsible for privacy policies, consent and age ratings. Related reading: rules for kids games and game age ratings.

    Recent findings suggest that state which country's law applies and how disputes are handled: negotiation first, then mediation or arbitration, then courts. Cross-border projects benefit from agreeing this early.

    We sign an NDA before discussing your idea, work in milestones with playable builds and assign 100 percent of the source and assets to you on payment. Details are on the offer page and in how to choose a game development studio.

    Related: Outsource game development · About the studio · Get a quote.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that in this article, we explore the top 10 AI tools that are driving innovation and efficiency in various industries.
    • Industry observers note that chatGPT is a large language model that generates human-like responses to a variety of prompts.
    • Overall, ChatGPT is a powerful tool for natural language processing, but it should be used with care and with an understanding of its limitations.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that in this article, we explore the top 10 AI tools that are driving innovation and efficiency in various industries. These tools are designed to automate repetitive tasks, improve workflow, and increase productivity. The tools included in our list are some of the most advanced and widely used in the market, and are suitable for a variety of applications. Some of the tools focus on natural language processing, such as ChatGPT and Grammarly, while others focus on image and video generation, such as DALL-E and Lumen5. Other tools such as OpenAI Codex, Tabnine, Canva, Jasper AI,, and Surfer SEO are designed to help with specific tasks such as code understanding content writing and website optimization. This list is a great starting point for anyone looking to explore the possibilities of AI and how it can be applied to their business or project.

    Industry observers note that chatGPT is a large language model that generates human-like responses to a variety of prompts. It can be used for tasks such as language translation, question answering, and text completion. It can handle a wide range of topics and styles of writing, and generates coherent and fluent text, but should be used with care as it may generate text that is biased, offensive, or factually incorrect.

    Overall, ChatGPT is a powerful tool for natural language processing, but it should be used with care and with an understanding of its limitations.

    It has been revealed that DALL-E is a generative model developed by OpenAI that is capable of generating images from text prompts. It is based on the GPT-3 architecture, which is a transformer-based neural network language model that has been trained on a massive dataset of text. DALL-E can generate images that are similar to a training dataset and it can generate high-resolution images that are suitable for commercial use.

    Industry observers note that overall, DALL-E is a powerful AI-based tool for generating images, it can be used for a variety of applications such as creating images for commercial use, gaming, and other creative projects. It is notable to note that the generated images should be reviewed and used with care, as they may not be entirely original and could be influenced by the training data.

    Lumen5 is a content creation platform that uses AI to help customers create videos, social media posts, and other types of content. It has several features that make it useful for content creation and marketing, including:.

    It has been revealed that overall, Lumen5 is a useful tool for creating content quickly and easily, it can help automate the process of creating videos, social media posts, and other types of content. However, the quality of the generated content may vary depending on the source material and it is important to review and edit the content before publishing it.

    Sources indicate that grammarly is a writing-enhancement platform that uses AI to check for grammar, punctuation, and spelling errors in the text. It also provides suggestions for improving the clarity, concision, and readability of the text. It has several features that make it useful for improving writing, including:.

    OpenAI Codex is a system developed by OpenAI that can create code from natural language descriptions of software tasks. The system is based on the GPT-3 model and can generate code in multiple programming languages.

    Overall, OpenAI Codex is a powerful tool that can help automate the process of writing code and make it more accessible to non-technical people.     #46137. JSON-LD in the Next.js App Router: typed, safe, in the initial HTML, and in sync with the page

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (504 w)

    JSON-LD in the Next.js App Router: typed, safe, in the initial HTML, and in sync with the page

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (504 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Structured data is one of the few SEO tasks that lands squarely on the developer's desk.
    • Here is a setup for the App Router that avoids the usual problems: the markup is typed, rendered on the server, escaped correctly, built from the same data as the visible page, and tested.
    • Sources indicate that structured data doesn't improve rankings by itself.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Structured data is one of the few SEO tasks that lands squarely on the developer's desk. Marketing asks for "schema", someone pastes a JSON-LD snippet from a generator into the layout, and a year later the price in the markup no longer matches the price on the page.

    Here is a setup for the App Router that avoids the usual problems: the markup is typed, rendered on the server, escaped correctly, built from the same data as the visible page, and tested.

    Sources indicate that structured data doesn't improve rankings by itself. It makes pages eligible for rich results such as product price and availability, breadcrumbs or article details, and it helps search engines understand the entities on a page. Google requires the markup to describe content that is visible on the page; markup that contradicts the page can cost eligibility.

    That last rule is the technical requirement hiding in an SEO guideline: the JSON-LD and the rendered page must come from the same source of truth.

    In a recent development, in the App Router, the simplest correct approach is a plain , it ends the tag early and whatever follows is parsed as HTML. Replacing < with its Unicode escape keeps the JSON valid and the document intact. The Next.js documentation recommends the same.

    The schema-dts package provides TypeScript types for the Schema.org vocabulary. It catches misspelled properties and wrong value types at build time. It does not know Google's rich result requirements, which are stricter per feature; a perfectly typed Product can still lack what Google needs for a product snippet. Types prevent typos, validators check eligibility.

    Site-wide entities like your organization and website belong in the root layout, and page-level entities can reference them instead of repeating them:.

    An article page can then set publisher: { "@id": "https://example.com/#organization" }. Stable @id values turn several disconnected blocks into one graph, which is easier to maintain and easier for consumers to interpret.

    Industry observers note that validators are manual tools. A small check against a preview deployment catches the regressions that matter: markup that disappeared, no longer parses, or lost a required field.

    In a recent development, run it against one URL per template. JSON.parse failing is a test failure too, which is exactly what you want.

    Recent findings suggest that run Google's Rich Results Test on a sample of each template after changes to the markup, and the Schema Markup Validator if you also care about general Schema.org validity. Then watch Search Console's enhancement reports for latest errors.

    Samples miss the errors that only occur on some products or categories, so a full crawl helps periodically. Crawl Foundry Site Audit validates detected markup on every crawled URL against Schema.org and Google's rich result requirements and groups recurring findings, which usually point to one template. See the Site Audit feature page.

    For which types are worth implementing and how they relate to rich results, the Crawl Foundry glossary entry on schema markup is a good companion to this post.

    #46134. Latest Update: Java4Shell: How to Check If You're Vulnerable (apt upgrade Misses Containers)

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1047 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

    Latest Update: Java4Shell: How to Check If You're Vulnerable (apt upgrade Misses Containers)

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1047 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that you ran apt upgrade openjdk-17-jdk, java -version printed a fresh build, and you went to lunch.
    • According to recent reports, java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938) is a heap overflow in HotSpot's AVX-512 Base64 decoder.
    • Below: which Java 17, 21, 25 and 27 builds are affected, which are fixed, and four commands that find every JVM on a host or in a container image, including the ones java -version never sees.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that you ran apt upgrade openjdk-17-jdk, java -version printed a fresh build, and you went to lunch. Your Keycloak container still runs its own JRE, your Jenkins agent image is pinned to last month's Temurin, and the vendor appliance in the corner has a JVM you have never seen a version string for.

    According to recent reports, java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938) is a heap overflow in HotSpot's AVX-512 Base64 decoder. Calif, who found it, rates it 9.2 under CVSS 4.0 and lists Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, Artifactory, Jenkins and PingFederate as pre-auth RCE in default configs. Oracle scores it 8.1 under CVSS 3.1, citing high attack complexity (Aikido). Patches shipped November 17, 2026.

    Below: which Java 17, 21, 25 and 27 builds are affected, which are fixed, and four commands that find every JVM on a host or in a container image, including the ones java -version never sees.

    Not in how easy it is to exploit. Log4Shell was one string in a User-Agent header. Here the overwritten bytes are a fixed pattern derived from the decoder, not attacker-chosen, and the Harness team didn't get code execution in their lab. With the default heap the write was silent across thousands of triggers; only after shrinking TLABs (-XX:TLABSize=2048 -XX:-ResizeTLAB) did they get a SIGSEGV in G1. Calif's own exploit is spray-and-retry heap grooming, and they say it is sensitive to RTT and jitter. On Lobsters someone called it "a nothingburger" next to Log4Shell, and the EPSS score quoted there was 0.00734.

    I still think it's the worst JVM bug since Log4Shell, for two reasons.

    First, the preconditions are boring. As a Lobsters commenter pointed out, Traefik, Envoy and HAProxy don't buffer requests by default, and Zen 4 shipped in 2022. And Base64 from strangers arrives before login all the time. Harness lists HTTP Basic headers, JWT segments decoded before the signature check, and SASL exchanges like Kafka SCRAM.

    Recent findings suggest that second, and this is the Log4Shell part, the fix lives in every copy of the runtime. Log4Shell at least came down to one dependency in a pom.xml. Here you have to hunt down every JVM you ship, and most teams have no list of those.

    Calif also claims finding the bug took about an hour and the first working exploit two more, for under $200 in token costs. They're holding back the per-product chains until people have upgraded. Aikido had seen no confirmed exploitation in the wild as of November 18. I wouldn't bet on that lasting.

    In a recent development, ARM64 is not affected. Graviton fleets can relax. EPYC Naples, Rome and Milan are AVX2-only, as one HN commenter noted, so older boxes are out of scope too.

    According to Aikido, standard Java 8 and 11 are not affected, with one exception: Oracle lists its Java SE 8 Enterprise Performance Pack build (8u511-perf) as vulnerable.

    Fixed builds, from Aikido's roundup:.

    According to recent reports, EOL lines are affected and don't get their own fix. Move 18-20 to 21, 22-24 to 25, and 26 to 27. Red Hat is expediting RHEL 8, 9 and 10 builds. Zulu and Microsoft number their builds differently, Aikido has no fixed build numbers for Liberica yet, and distro packages carry their own versioning, so check each vendor's advisory and don't eyeball it against Oracle's table.

    Sources indicate that one Temurin gotcha: Adoptium publishes the binaries per platform as testing finishes, and the Docker Hub images only follow once every binary for that version is out. Your FROM eclipse-temurin:17-jre rebuild may pull the old JRE for a while.

    This one is from Calif's writeup:.

    All four flags need to show up. If any are missing, this host can't hit the vulnerable path. But your autoscaling group can land the same image on a Sapphire Rapids node tomorrow, so don't treat a clean dev box as proof about production.

    Every JDK, JRE and jlink-built runtime has a release file at its root. Reading those files covers bundled runtimes without executing anything:.

    This is where the surprises turn up: /opt//jre, jpackage'd desktop tools, an IDE's bundled runtime, the copy your monitoring agent brought along.

    According to recent reports, the binary on disk doesn't matter if the process still has the old one loaded. Harness's advice is to check the running process rather than trust the image tag. Finding processes by name misses custom launchers, so match on libjvm.so instead:.

    For each hit, jcmd VM.version tells you the build, and jcmd VM.flags -all | grep -E 'UseBASE64Intrinsics|UseAVX' tells you whether the fast path is on. To see what a particular binary defaults to on this CPU:.

    UseBASE64Intrinsics true and UseAVX at 3 on a VBMI-capable host means you're exposed until you patch.

    Distroless images don't have a shell or find, so don't bother with docker exec. Export the filesystem and read the release file out of the tarball:.

    For Kubernetes, kubectl get pods -A -o jsonpath='{..image}' | tr ' ' '\n' | sort -u gives you the image list to feed into the same loop.

    Harness also published a runtime checker script that compares local JDKs against the advisory builds and checks the CPU and flags; exit code 2 means a JDK is still exposed. Their post indicates it as curl | bash. Read it before you pipe it into a root shell on prod.

    Calif lists both of these flags as workarounds and still tells everyone to patch right away.

    Strict Base64 validation in front of the decoder (length a multiple of 4, alphabet only, padding only at the end) is a backstop. Harness notes that a loose character-class check doesn't catch the inputs that overflow.

    Switching to ZGC isn't a fix either. The only exploit discussed so far targets G1, but as one Lobsters commenter pointed out, the bug isn't in G1 and can still be used for denial of service under ZGC.

    My order would be: internet-facing services that decode Base64 before auth (SSO, CI, artifact repos) first, then image rebuilds, then the appliances you'll have to open vendor tickets for.

    In a recent development, did your scan find a Java runtime you didn't know you were running? Where was it hiding? And if you think the Log4Shell comparison is overblown, make your case in the comments.

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Org ↗ Open Full Page

    What Happier People Tend To Believe About Others

    📅 30 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (644 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Org

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • A review involving over 2.5 million people links one social outlook to greater happiness—and the connection runs both ways.
    • A review involving over 2.5 million people links one social outlook to greater happiness—and the connection runs both ways.
    • Trusting others is linked to greater happiness and life satisfaction, a review involving over 2.5 million people finds.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A review involving over 2.5 million people links one social outlook to greater happiness—and the connection runs both ways.

    A review involving over 2.5 million people links one social outlook to greater happiness—and the connection runs both ways.

    Trusting others is linked to greater happiness and life satisfaction, a review involving over 2.5 million people finds.

    Happier people also tend to become more trusting over time.

    The link between trust and happiness is slightly stronger in children, adolescents and older adults, possibly because supportive relationships are especially key at these ages.

    Trust may help meet the need to belong by making it easier to build relationships in which people feel supported and secure.

    The research combined almost 1,000 findings from studies involving people aged six to 84.

    The analysis examined how trust related to everyday emotions, including happiness and sadness, as well as people’s overall satisfaction with their lives.

    Greater trust was consistently associated with better wellbeing.

    The association was somewhat stronger among children and adolescents than among young and middle-aged adults, and stronger among older adults than young adults.

    Trust may matter more at ages when people are building close relationships or becoming more dependent on others.

    For younger people, learning whom to trust is part of building meaningful friendships and supportive social networks.

    In later life, people may prioritise a smaller circle of close relationships and depend more on others for support.

    The researchers distinguished between trust in familiar people, trust in people generally and trust in institutions.

    The first involves confidence in someone known personally, such as a partner, friend or relative.

    General trust involves expectations about people more broadly, including strangers, while institutional trust concerns organisations such as governments, banks and the police.

    All three were associated with better wellbeing, but trust in familiar people showed the strongest connection.

    Trust may support wellbeing partly because close relationships require a willingness to be vulnerable.

    Expecting someone to respond with care can make it easier to seek help, cooperate and maintain a supportive connection.

    These relationships may satisfy the basic psychological need to feel connected to others and cared for in return.

    Trust could also provide a broader sense of security and predictability, making the social world feel more dependable.

    This may help explain why trust was slightly more closely related to overall life satisfaction than to positive or negative emotions.

    Life satisfaction reflects a broader assessment of how life is going, whereas emotions can fluctuate with immediate experiences.

    The relationship also worked in the other direction, with greater wellbeing predicting more trust later.

    One proposed explanation is that emotions influence how people interpret the world around them.

    Feeling happy may encourage more positive perceptions of other people, while anxiety may draw attention towards threats and uncertainty.

    Trust and wellbeing could therefore reinforce each other, with supportive expectations helping people feel better and positive feelings making trust easier.

    The wider social environment mattered too, with a stronger connection between trust and wellbeing in countries where people were generally more trusting.

    A trusting outlook may be more beneficial when the people around us are dependable.

    Simply encouraging someone to trust more overlooks the behaviour of the people and institutions receiving that trust.

    Professor Catrin Finkenauer, study co-author, said:.

    “But trust can’t be forced—it has to be earned.”.

    The findings therefore highlight the importance of honesty, reliability, transparency and fair treatment in relationships and institutions.

    “When we build trust, we also support mental health and stronger communities.”.

    The study was published in the journal Psychological Bulletin (Bi et al., 2025).

    Recent findings suggest that psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog.     What sets LimeWire apart is its seamless integration of different AI models and design styles. Owners have the flexibility to effortlessly switch between various AI models, exploring diverse design styles such as cinematic, digital art, pixel art, anime, analog film, and more. Each style imparts a distinctive visual identity to the generated AI art, enabling users to explore a broad spectrum of creative possibilities.

    Sources indicate that the platform also offers additional features, including samplers, allowing people to fine-tune the quality and detail levels of their creations. Customization options and prompt guidance further enhance the user experience, providing a user-friendly interface for both novice and experienced creators.

    Recent findings suggest that excitingly, LimeWire is actively developing its proprietary AI model, signaling ongoing innovation and enhancements to its image generation capabilities. This upcoming addition holds the promise of further expanding the creative horizons for LimeWire customers, making it an evolving and dynamic platform within the landscape of AI-driven art and image creation.

    Upon completing your creative endeavor on LimeWire, the platform allows you the option to publish your content. An intriguing feature follows this step: LimeWire automates the process of minting your creation as a Non-Fungible Token (NFT), utilizing either the Polygon or Algorand blockchain. This transformative step imbues your artwork with a unique digital signature, securing its authenticity and ownership in the decentralized realm.

    Creators on LimeWire hold the power to decide the accessibility of their NFT creations. By opting for a public release, the content becomes discoverable by anyone, fostering a space for engagement and interaction. Furthermore, this choice opens the avenue for enthusiasts to trade the NFTs, adding a layer of community involvement to the artistic journey.

    Additionally, you can earn ad revenue from your content creations as well.

    When you publish content on LimeWire, you will receive 70% of all ad revenue from other customers who view your images, music, and videos on the platform.

    Sources indicate that this revenue model will be much more beneficial to designers. You can experiment with the AI image and content generation tools and share your creations while earning a small income on the side.

    The revenue you earn from your creations will come in the form of LMWR tokens, LimeWire’s own cryptocurrency.

    Your earnings will be paid every month in LMWR, which you can then trade on many popular crypto exchange platforms like Kraken, ByBit, and UniSwap.

    You can also use your LMWR tokens to pay for prompts when using LimeWire generative AI tools.

    For $9.99 per month, you will get 1,000 credits per month, up to 2 ,000 image generations, early access to upcoming AI models, and 50% ad revenue share.

    For $29 per month, you will get 3750 credits per month, up to 7500 image generations, early access to new AI models, and 60% ad revenue share.

    For $49 per month, you will get 5,000 credits per month, up to 10,000 image generations, early access to fresh AI models, and 70% ad revenue share.

    For $99 per month, you will get 11,250 credits per month, up to 2 2,500 image generations, early access to new AI models, and 70% ad revenue share.

    With all premium intends, you will receive a Pro profile badge, full creation history, faster image generation, and no ads.

    It has been revealed that in conclusion, LimeWire emerges as a democratizing force in the creative landscape, providing an inclusive platform where anyone can unleash their artistic potential and effortlessly share their work. With the integration of AI, LimeWire eliminates traditional barriers, empowering designers, musicians, and artists to publish their creations and earn revenue with just a few clicks.

    The ongoing commitment of LimeWire to innovation is evident in its aims to enhance generative AI tools with upcoming features and models. The upcoming expansion to include music and video generation tools holds the promise of unlocking even more possibilities for creators. It sparks anticipation about the diverse and innovative ways in which artists will leverage these tools to produce and publish their own unique creations.

    According to recent reports, for those eager to explore, LimeWire's AI tools are readily accessible for free, providing an opportunity to experiment and delve into the world of generative art. As LimeWire continues to evolve, creators are encouraged to stay tuned for the launch of its forthcoming AI music and video generation tools, promising a future brimming with creative potential and endless artistic exploration.

    Industry observers note that looking to level up your content creation game in 2025? You're in the right place! The digital landscape has evolved dramatically, and AI tools have become essential for creators who want to stay ahead of the curve. In this guide, I'll show you the top 10 AI tools that are revolutionizing content creation and making creators' lives easier.

    Why You Need These AI Tools in 2025.

    Content creation has become more demanding than ever. Whether you're a social media influencer, marketer, or business owner, keeping up with the constant need for fresh, engaging content can be overwhelming. That's where AI tools come in – they're not just fancy tech, they're your secret weapon for creating better content faster.

    Let's Dive Into the Top 10 AI Tools for 2025.

    Sources indicate that what Makes It Special: ChatGPT has evolved into a comprehensive content creation assistant by combining advanced language understanding with specialized content optimization features. Its ability to generate, edit, and optimize content while maintaining brand voice and industry expertise makes it an essential tool for creators who need to produce high-quality written content at scale.

    What Makes It Special: Canva Magic Studio has transformed the graphic design landscape by combining its user-friendly interface with powerful AI capabilities. The platform's ability to understand design principles and automatically generate on-brand content while maintaining professional aesthetics makes it accessible for beginners while providing enough sophistication for professional designers.

    Perfect For: Small businesses, social media managers, and anyone needing quick, professional-looking designs.

    What Makes It Special: RunwayML stands out as the ultimate video creation powerhouse by combining professional-grade effects with user-friendly AI technology. Its game-changing ability to manipulate video content – from changing weather effects with a text prompt to removing objects seamlessly in real-time – makes it indispensable for creators who want to produce high-quality video content without getting bogged down by technical complexities.

    Perfect For: Video creators, YouTubers, and social media managers who want to create professional-quality videos swiftly.

    Sources indicate that what Makes It Special: Midjourney V6 has redefined AI image generation by mastering the nuances of professional photography and artistic style. Its ability to understand and execute complex creative directions – from specific lighting conditions to branded visual styles – while maintaining consistent quality across multiple generations makes it the go-to tool for creators who need stunning visuals that align perfectly with their brand identity.

    Perfect For: Social media managers, digital marketers, and anyone needing professional-quality visuals consistently.

    In a recent development, what Makes It Special: Synthesia has transformed video creation by making it possible to create professional-looking AI avatar videos in minutes. Its ability to generate natural-looking presentations in multiple languages with synchronized lip movements and gestures makes it invaluable for creators who need to produce video content at scale without the traditional filming process.

    Perfect For: Businesses and educators creating training videos, presentations, and multilingual content.

    What Makes It Special: Descript has transformed audio and video editing by making it as simple as editing a text document. Its innovative approach to media editing, combined with powerful AI features like automatic transcription and filler word removal, makes professional-quality editing accessible to creators of all skill levels.

    Perfect For: Podcasters, video creators, and teams needing efficient audio/video editing solutions.

    What Makes It Special: ElevenLabs has revolutionized voice synthesis by achieving unprecedented levels of natural speech quality and emotional expression. Its ability to clone voices accurately and generate multiple languages with proper accents and inflections makes it the ultimate tool for creators who need professional-quality voiceovers without the traditional recording process or voice actor limitations.

    Perfect For: Podcasters, video creators, and content creators needing professional voiceovers in multiple languages.

    What Makes It Special: Tribescaler brings a scientific approach to viral content creation by combining trend analysis with content optimization. Its powerful AI engine analyzes successful content patterns across platforms and provides actionable insights to help creators craft content that's more likely to go viral, while maintaining authenticity and audience engagement.

    Perfect For: Content creators and social media managers focused on maximizing reach and engagement.

    It has been revealed that what Makes It Special: Clickable revolutionizes ad creation by seamlessly blending data-driven insights with creative automation. Its ability to analyze brand assets and automatically generate platform-optimized ad variations while maintaining brand voice transforms the tedious process of ad creation into a streamlined, results-driven workflow that consistently delivers high-performing content.

    Perfect For: Digital marketers and businesses looking to scale their ad production efficiently.

    What Makes It Special: CopyAI has established itself as a powerhouse in AI-powered copywriting by offering specialized content generation for various marketing formats. Its sophisticated understanding of marketing psychology and brand voice, combined with its ability to generate compelling copy across multiple formats and industries, makes it invaluable for marketers and content creators who need to produce engaging, conversion-focused content at scale.

    Perfect For: Marketing teams, copywriters, and businesses needing high-converting marketing copy across multiple channels.

    The AI tools listed here are revolutionizing the content creation landscape in 2025, making it easier than ever to produce high-quality, engaging, and impactful content. By integrating these tools into your workflow, you can save time, unleash your creativity, and achieve better results.

    It has been revealed that AI doesn't replace creativity; it amplifies it. As a content creator, your unique voice and vision are irreplaceable. These tools serve as enablers, helping you focus on what you do best—creating. Explore, experiment, and innovate. The future of content creation is here, and it's brimming with possibilities.

    According to recent reports, embrace these technologies, stay ahead of the curve, and watch your creative potential soar. The only limit is your imagination!

    How To Build The Ultimate Aldi Charcuterie Board For Under $25

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2281 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foodrepublic

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that everybody loves a charcuterie board, because a charcuterie board has a little something for everybody.
    • Charcuterie boards can add up rapidly and can cost a fortune to throw together...
    • Recent findings suggest that need some ideas?
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that everybody loves a charcuterie board, because a charcuterie board has a little something for everybody. But there's a certain art to building a good charcuterie board. A good board is one that offers up an array of different flavors, textures, and colors — each one complimenting the next — all coming together harmoniously to provide the ultimate grazing experience.

    Charcuterie boards can add up rapidly and can cost a fortune to throw together... but it's perfectly possible to create a great charcuterie board that doesn't break the bank. It all depends where you shop, and one of the best (and most affordable) places you can find your ingredients is at Aldi. In fact, you can build many a beautiful, bountiful board with just $25 thanks to Aldi's highly-rated cheeses, selection of essential cured meats, fresh fruit, crackers, and many more of Aldi's must-have products.

    Recent findings suggest that need some ideas? We've got plenty of ways to build the ultimate charcuterie board that stay within this humble budget to to help make you the host with the most. Note that all of the products and prices below are sourced from an Aldi location in southern California and inventory may vary throughout the country, so be sure to double check your local store's online inventory.

    In a recent development, if you want to stick to the tried and true, classic charcuterie board ingredients, you can gather all the hits at Aldi for $25 and build a beautiful board. First (and arguable the most crucial) stop is the cheese. With Aldi's affordable prices, you can feature three different cheeses which will give the board enough variety — ideally, a classic board combines both soft and hard cheese.

    Aldi's private-label brand Emporium Selection has three different cheeses that will not only go together lovely, but will satisfy different tastes and preferences: The Garlic & Herb Gourmet Spreadable Cheese, the Smoked Gouda Cheese, and the Aged Reserved White Cheddar Cheese (it's America's favorite cheese, after all).

    Industry observers note that when it comes to the meat, you can't go wrong with a Salami Trio; you'll get the most bang for your buck here by being able to offer three different types of salami on your board (Black Peppercorn, Smoked Calabrese, and Double Smoked Salami). And now that you have the main events, it's just a matter of filling the board in with two more essential items. Grapes will add some freshness and sweetness, complimenting the salty meat and cheese, Aldi's Rosemary Flatbread Crackers will be the perfect accompaniment for everything else.

    If you're looking to serve up something more seasonal, Aldi is full of great fall finds that will work splendidly on a charcuterie board. And thanks to the extremely reasonable prices, you can actually cram a lot of different items onto this board so that it's overflowing with fall flavors.

    It has been revealed that starting with your cheeses, three seasonal picks will be the centerpieces: a Cheddar Parmesan Cheese ($3.95) that will go with all of your other flavors, a 1,000 Day Aged Gouda ($3.99) for that sharp bite, and a Crimson Cranberry White Stilton ($4.19) to really bring it home. For the meat, Aldi's Honey & Bourbon Cocktail Salami ($3.29) is the perfect choice to bring in some of those comforting fall notes.

    According to recent reports, candied Pecans ($4.39) and Fig Fruit Spread ($3.29) will add some sweetness to the board, and you can brighten things up a bit with a few fresh seasonal Bartlett Pears ($3.29). Grab some of Aldi's Sea Salt Scalloped Crackers ($1.99) that'll work perfectly with any combo, and you've got yourself one great fall-flavored charcuterie board.

    According to recent reports, are you cooking up an Italian dinner, or just in the mood for some salty, briny antipasti appetizers? You can create a charcuterie board version of Italian antipasti with several Italian-inspired favorites that you can find at Aldi, and snack like you're in Italy while keeping it all under $25.

    For your cheese selection, a fresh log of mozzarella cheese ($3.25) will be the perfect counterpart to the nutty, salty authentic Parmigiano-Reggiano ($6.05) (which is different from Parmesan). And with several types of Italian-imported cured meats available, you can offer up some options like Priano's Prosciutto Italiano ($3.55) and Speck Italiano ($3.55).

    Outside of the meat and cheese, Aldi actually has a ready-made medley of antipasti olives ($2.85) which includes black and green pitted olives, provolone cheese cubes, button mushrooms, and roasted red peppers — giving your board lots of variety and bang for your buck. Aldi's Artichoke Bruschetta ($3.09) is the perfect dip-able, spreadable item to accompany everything, along with some Sea Salt & Olive Oil Italian Breadsticks ($2.19) for crispy, crunchy bites.

    Industry observers note that if you're feeling a little French, bring some French countryside charm to a rustic charcuterie board using an array of Aldi products that will give your guests a little taste of France. Because who doesn't want that?

    You can go for the French trifecta of cheeses for this one: a double creme brie ($4.39), a buttery camembert ($4.39), and a smoked Gruyere ($4.39). This will give your board a mix of soft and hard cheeses, each with its own unique flavor to keep the tastebuds on their toes. Stick to a classic salami to compliment the bolder flavors of the cheese, and if you want to level things up you can always bake the brie (which you can even do in your microwave).

    Then include some classic French ingredients for those added touches that'll transport you to France. Aldi's Herb Cornichons ($3.29) and Burman's Sweet Honey Dijon Mustard ($1.75) will taste delicious served alongside your meat and cheese, and then you can freshen things up a bit with red grapes ($1.69 / pound). Now all you need is the perfect vehicle to carry all of these French goodies: Aldi's Original Brioche Style Mini Toasts ($1.89).

    One last stop in the Mediterranean. You can combine all of the delicious Mediterranean-inspired items at Aldi to build a board that transforms charcuterie into a delectable mezze spread.

    According to recent reports, when it comes to the cheese, there's one clear star here: feta. You can represent it two ways in one board by grabbing the Tomato and Basil Feta Cheese Block ($3.95) and the Greek Feta Salad ($2.59) (made with Kalamata and green olives and cubes of feta marinated in herbs and spices). And the Dry Aged Fennel Mediterranean Style Salami ($3.99) is the no-brainer choice for this board's protein.

    Industry observers note that from there, focus on the delicious dips that make mezze what it is. Go for Aldi's Olive Tapenade Hummus ($2.85) to double down on those salty olives, and brighten up the board with a Cucumber Dill Tzatziki Dip ($3.29) made with Greek yogurt. Throw in some Deli-Sliced Roasted Red Peppers ($3.19) as an accompaniment, and don't forget everyone's favorite part: The pita bread ($2.85)! Pro tip: Throw 'em in the oven for a few minutes and serve them warm; it makes all the difference.

    Make the holidays even more festive with a holiday-themed charcuterie board that'll look (and taste) the part. Whether you're looking to serve something beautiful at your holiday party or you want to dive into those festive flavors while you can, Aldi has tons of options to choose from that scream holiday season.

    Recent findings suggest that start with Aldi's Cranberry Cinnamon Flavored Goat Cheese Log ($3.85) (because what claims holiday more than that combo?), and balance it out with the Cabot Seriously Sharp Cheddar Cheese for that sharpness everyone wants on a charcuterie board, plus some extra creaminess in the Double Crème Brie Cheese ($4.39). For the cured meat, you can stick with a classic prosciutto ($3.59), and accompany the main events with some warm and cozy flavors like Aldi's Caramelized Red Onion Chutney ($2.99) for sweetness and Honey Roasted Nut Blend ($5.29) for extra crunch.

    It has been revealed that pair everything with Aldi's Rosemary Artisan Crackers ($3.49) (bonus points if you have some real rosemary to use as decor). And, last but not least, choose a tasty whole pomegranate ($1.89) to give your board a pop of sweetness as well as a pop of color — leave one half in tact and place it on your board cut-side open; it'll look beautiful. Here's how to pick the best pomegranate for your board.

    Okay, so this may not technically qualify as a charcuterie board, but that term tends to be very forgiving these days. For all those veggie lovers out there, you can build a meatless, vegetable-forward board at Aldi that'll give everyone a fresh taste of the garden and still keep things interesting.

    Recent findings suggest that aldi's Roasted Garlic & Tomato Basil Monterey Jack Cheese ($3.49) and Onion & Chive Double Gloucester Cheese ($4.19) are a great duo to anchor this board, and a Spinach Artichoke Dip ($2.99) adds even more flavor and creaminess. Along with Aldi's Garden Vegetable Crackers ($1.79), you can serve up all of your herby, cheesy goodness with some fresh crudités using Gourmet Mixed Baby Carrots ($2.99) (which happen to be adorable) and a pound of radishes ($1.45) for added crisp and color. For that last flavorful munch, throw in the Garlic & Herb Nut Blend ($5.29), which includes seasoned pecans, almonds, and cashews.

    Industry observers note that charcuterie can be a morning thing too! When it comes to brunch, pretty much anything goes... so why not turn the meal into a flavorful board of breakfast delights? This one gets a little creative and combines sweet, salty, herby, and smoky for the perfect brunch munching.

    Sources indicate that instead of your typical bread or crackers, you can build this board around Aldi's mini bagels ($3.85), which will be the perfect vehicle for soft, herby cheeses like everybody's favorite Boursin Garlic & Fine Herb Cheese ($6.05) and a Chive & Onion Cream Cheese Spread ($1.99). Make it a lox party by adding some of Aldi's Cold Smoked Atlantic Salmon ($4.39) so your guests can create their perfect combo. To round it all out, opt for the jam or preserves of your choice (we like blueberry preserves, $3.09) and incorporate some fresh blackberries ($1.69) to give everyone their morning serving of fruit.

    Some like it hot, and those people can find plenty of options at Aldi to set their mouths on fire. Make things (painfully) fun with a spiced-up charcuterie board featuring some of Aldi's hot and spicy products.

    According to recent reports, begin the spice-loving journey with Aldi's 3 Chili Gouda Cheese ($3.85) paired with the Tequila & Ghost Pepper Cocktail Salami ($3.29): A killer combo. Next, grab the Stuffed Green Pepperoncini ($3.99) — these will be a great addition because they're a little briny and spicy, but they're made with Herbes de Provence and filled with cream cheese, which will offer a bit of a respite from the heat.

    Now for the dips, include the Hot Honey Dip ($2.79) for a bit of sweet heat, and the Piquillo Pepper & Artichoke Bruschetta ($3.09) for another delicious element that offers a bit more sweetness than spice to balance things out. Finish it all off with Aldi's Sea Salt & Pepper Scalloped Crackers ($1.99) for dipping and dunking.

    Sources indicate that pickled and pickle-flavored foods seem to be all the rage lately, so why not lean in? Turn your party into a pickle party by building a fully pickled-out charcuterie board at Aldi for that punchy hit of briny, vinegary goodness.

    Two types of cheese will be at the center of the pickle party: the Dill Havarti Cheese ($2.75) (a creamy Danish-style cheese) will keep you on theme while the Extra Sharp Fresh York Cheddar Cheese Cubes ($3.29) will cut all that vinegar with salty sharpness. The Appleton Farms Gourmet Deli Selection ($5.89) is a great choice for your cured meat because it gives you three types of meat in one package (Pepper Salami, Hot Capocollo, and Hot Calabrese).

    According to recent reports, from there, you obviously need some actual pickles. Go for Great Gherkins Kosher Baby Whole Dill Pickles ($2.09), which are the perfect size for snacking. Add in Happy Harvest Sliced Pickled Beets ($2.19) for more color and variety, and Aldi's Dill Dip ($3.99) made with sour cream and dill for something delicious and creamy to dip into. Stick to Aldi's Original Crisp Crackers ($1.79) to accompany everything so your cracker doesn't compete with all of the flavors you've already got going on.

    According to recent reports, lastly, for all those out there with a sweet tooth, there are lots of ways to incorporate notes of sweetness into your "charcuterie" board while still keeping it fairly savory (this one foregoes the meat as well). If you love sweet but don't want to go full dessert board, this board is for you.

    Recent findings suggest that the Cocoa Cardona Cheese ($4.95) at Aldi is a goat's milk cheese with a cocoa powder rind, giving you just a hint of chocolate, and the Honey I'd Rather Bee at the Sea Sea Salt Honey Cheddar Cheese ($3.85) also offers a delicate balance of sweet and salty. And the Chocolate Chip Cannoli Dip ($3.29), decidedly more sweet than savory, is a cream cheese-base dip that'll go perfectly with Benton's Belgian Butter Waffle Crisps ($2.19).

    For your board's accouterments, Simply Nature Dark Chocolate Covered Freeze Dried Strawberries ($4.39) are a delicious addition to munch on, as are the Choceur Dark Peanut Choc Clusters ($3.49) which add a bit more salt to the mix. Lastly, you can't go wrong with some fresh raspberries ($2.59).

    Add This Fresh Herb To Your Bowl Of Chili For 10x The Flavor (Thanks, Ina Garten)

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (431 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Foodrepublic

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that A bowl of chili welcomes a wide array of renditions.
    • Using the Mediterranean herb in the Tex-Mex recipe may sound unusual, but the flavors align surprisingly well.
    • Garten's rendition works the basil into a tomato sauce base, full of sweet bell peppers and onions, lightly recalling a pasta sauce in composition.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that A bowl of chili welcomes a wide array of renditions. You can make the dish red or green, use proteins like turkey, pork, or chicken instead of the classic beef, and include many aromatics in the mix. Each detail makes a chili rendition unique. Even a fresh herb gives a bowl a whole newly introduced character — just look toward Ina Garten's inclusion of basil. Ina Garten often uses basil as a swap for cilantro, so her inclusion of the herb in her chili makes sense.

    Using the Mediterranean herb in the Tex-Mex recipe may sound unusual, but the flavors align surprisingly well. Garten uses basil's mildly citrusy sweet and lightly peppery flavor specifically in a chicken-based chili, integrating the herb during both the initial simmering stage and as a final garnish. It's a one-two combo that establishes an herbal character that infuses into every bite, lending more than just a basil-inflected finish.

    Garten's rendition works the basil into a tomato sauce base, full of sweet bell peppers and onions, lightly recalling a pasta sauce in composition. Still, seasonings like cumin, chili powder, and a dash of spicy cayenne appear in the mix, cementing the dish as a bowl of chili, only brighter and more herbal in nature.

    Ina Garten's tips for cooking chicken perfectly dependably deliver, but don't rule out employing the basil in chili recipes with other proteins, too. The herb also works well in an extra-hearty bean and brisket rendition that's spiced with chiles and even coffee. Cooked down right alongside the kidney beans, basil lends the legumes its distinct herbal character, all without becoming a cornerstone flavor. You can try out such a technique in a classic ground beef chili, too; using the herb early in cooking makes it one of many layered flavors.

    If you're after a more basil-forward spin, consider working the herb into a ground turkey chili recipe. You can still go heavy on the spice, using chili powder and jalapeños alongside garlic powder and cumin. Add dried basil early on and raw basil atop the finished chili, and you'll get a delicate bowl, herbal-tasting and fresh, yet still pretty classic.

    And for a more inventive approach, take a page from Thai cuisine, specifically Phat ka-phrao (stir-fried basil beef). Made with sturdier Thai basil, this version of the herb stands up better to heat. Saute the meat alongside extra-spicy chiles, lots of garlic, and this type of basil, and you can lay down the foundation for an extra-bold chili, still delicious over rice or with tortilla chips.

    #46118. How I Get Free Traffic from ChatGPT in 2025 (AIO vs SEO)
