    We’ve all been there. January 1st hits, and you decide this is the year you’re going to change your life and become the best version of yourself with some New Year’s resolutions. You might optimistically think, “You know what? I’m going to be healthier this year! I’m only going to drink on the weekends.”.

    Recent findings suggest that then two weeks later, on a Wednesday, you have the most stressful day at your job and you find yourself pouring a huge glass of wine. You’re instantly filled with regret for breaking your resolution and vow to never do them again because they don’t work and are clearly designed to make you feel disappointed.

    Take a deep breath. Resolutions don’t have to be this big set up for failure that feel impossible to keep. They can be as big or as small as you want them to be. We’ve put together a list of 60 mindful resolutions that are less about striving for perfection or making huge changes in your life, and more about slowly helping you to grow and build better habits in an achievable way. Sounds nice, right?

    So let’s ditch our list of impossible goals and jump into 60 resolutions that could help you thrive in 2027.

    Recent findings suggest that at the end of the year, many of us step back and realize that we feel really disconnected from a lot of the people in our life. We get busy and stuck in our own little world. It’s too easy for connections with our family, friends, partners, or coworkers to dwindle from time to time.

    Recent findings suggest that if this sounds familiar, here are 15 resolutions that can help you build more fulfilling relationships so that your support networks are there for you when you need it. (And you’re there for them when they need it too.).

    Pro tip: you don’t need to do all of 15. Just try choosing a few that feel good to you and then take some small steps towards adding them into your routine.

    Make a habit of giving your full attention to the people who matter most to you. Try planning regular (or semi-regular) family dinners, date nights, or hangs with friends. If you like phone calls, those work great too. (Just make sure you’re fully present!).

    When someone’s talking to you, focus fully on what they’re saying instead of thinking about your reply or what you’re going to eat for your next meal (we’ve all been there). Active listening reveals respect to your loved one and can help deepen your bond. If you want to get better at active listening, here are eight techniques to help.

    Too often, we take those around us for granted, so let the people in your life know you appreciate them. Saying something as easy as, “thank you” or writing a cute little note can let your loved one know how much they mean to you and make them feel good. Who doesn’t want to make their loved one feel good?

    Sources indicate that if you love them, say it. Life’s too short! Telling someone you love them is powerful and can help you grow a stronger bond. If you have people in your life like a macho uncle or disengaged cousin who have a hard time saying I love you, be the first to jump in and show them that it’s okay to express your affection for one another.

    Recent findings suggest that if you notice someone struggling in your life, step in and help. It doesn't need to be revolutionary. It could be helping with laundry or simply being there to listen. Just letting them know that you see their efforts and want to help can make a huge difference.

    Relationships are work. And in order for them to work, you need to put time into them. So set a reminder to check in with your loved ones, especially the ones you don’t see often. A quick text or call can do the trick and help you stay connected with your favorite people. And if you have folks in your life who are struggling, or who experience loneliness, make an extra effort to reach out and show you care.

    Don’t let misunderstandings grow. When you’re upset with someone, bring it up to them calmly and kindly, and with the goal of finding a solution. It can help to lead with “I feel” statements. And if your feelings are hurt over an innocent misunderstanding, start with, “I know you didn’t mean to hurt my feelings but,” so the other person knows they’re not in trouble and you want to come to a place of understanding.

    In a recent development, this might sound obvious, but if your loved one has good news, show genuine excitement for the good things that are happening for them. We all feel good when others celebrate with us. So send those flowers — almost no one’s going to get mad at you for sending flowers. Sometimes celebrating success for others feels hard if you feel stuck in your life, but by genuinely finding happiness for others, you may feel the glow of that happiness yourself.

    Sources indicate that use conversions with others as a time to genuinely disconnect from technology and focus on being together. When you’re spending time with someone, keep your phone in your pocket, in your purse, or somewhere that’s not in your hand. Give your loved one your full attention. This will make them feel seen and it helps you to stay more in the moment and form deeper connections.

    Recent findings suggest that everyone loves to feel seen and valued. Sometimes just surprising someone you love with a small gesture can make their day. It doesn’t have to be big, it could just be showing up to a hang with your loved one’s favorite snack, their preferred coffee drink, or even a small bouquet of flowers. Trying to be better about budgeting? Handwritten cards, or homemade crafts also make lovely surprises.

    It has been revealed that when someone you care about is struggling, before reacting, take a moment to put yourself in their shoes and understand what they might be going through. This can be a lot easier said than done, but try to treat them the way you would want to be treated —  with kindness instead of judgment.

    💙 If Empathy doesn’t come easy for you, check out this meditation from Tamara Levitt’s Relationships with Others series.

    It has been revealed that we all have preferences for how we like to give and receive love and it’s so special when the people in our lives make an effort to communicate affection in the ways we most appreciate. So take some time to understand a partner, family member, or friends love languages (here’s an overview of all five and how to identify yours). Showing love in the ways they like can make you closer. (And probably earn you brownie points!).

    Industry observers note that say yes to an invite or an activity you wouldn’t normally do. Stepping out of your comfort zone can help you feel energized and open you up to new experiences and learnings about yourself. The one time when it’s okay not to say yes is if you’re establishing boundaries with your emotional energy or time. It’s all about balance!

    While saying yes is great (see above), saying no is also key. Make an effort to have healthy relationships with solid boundaries. Tell people what you need, like alone time or limits on work talk. And respect their boundaries too. If all of that sounds tough, check out these six tips to setting healthy boundaries in your relationships.

    Recent findings suggest that humans make mistakes and the best thing you can do is to acknowledge them, learn and grow. So try to take responsibility if you make a mistake. You’ll feel free of guilt and you won’t have to double down on something you probably didn’t mean to do in the first place (like a bad joke that hurt someone’s feelings, or a meeting you were super late for.) A heartfelt apology can mend any damage and show your maturity (these seven tips will help you do it).

    Sources indicate that doesn’t it feel like we’re always trying to find a better work-life balance, get promoted, improve our work ethic, and feel more fulfilled with the work we’re doing? That constant desire for some sort of growth or change can be overwhelming and leave you not knowing where to start.

    So we’ve put together 15 work resolutions that might be more sustainable and rewarding for you — and will hopefully make the whole process feel less overwhelming.

    Protecting your personal time is so important for avoiding burnout, so decide on clear work hours and stick to them. Try setting a goal for logging off by 6pm or not looking at emails in your off time. If your job doesn’t currently give you the freedom to set these boundaries, chat with your superiors and express your goals where work-life balance is concerned.

    It has been revealed that organize your workspace to reduce clutter. A working area that you like (or at least doesn’t cause more stress) can really improve your mood and your focus. Once you reduce the clutter and get rid of any items that aren’t sparking joy, you could mindfully add things that feel good like a plant, photo, or a comfy chair.

    Large projects can be overwhelming. Try breaking them down into smaller, more manageable steps to make them less daunting and help you stay on track. You can also practice time-boxing to keep your focus — here’s how to do it .

    It has been revealed that go for a five-minute walk, enjoy a cup or tea, or do a quick stretch. It doesn’t really matter what you do on a break, just that you do something to rest your mind and give your body a little love. Set reminders if it’ll help you remember. (Here are 20 ways to take a mindful break.).

    Recent findings suggest that start each day by identifying your top three priorities. If you focus on the most important tasks first, this will help you make progress where it matters most. Got a few things on your to-do list that aren’t time sensitive? Resist the temptation to try to get them done when you’re exhausted and bump them to tomorrow when you can focus.

    According to recent reports, just like you want to celebrate the achievements of the people in your life, it’s equally vital to celebrate yourself! Take note of all of your accomplishments. This can help boost your confidence, help you stay motivated, and even make you smile.

    In a recent development, making upcoming friends isn’t just for your school years. Make an effort to connect with coworkers or other people in your field. Getting coffee with colleagues can help you build relationships and even help with career growth. You might find that your career is more fulfilling when you have solid relationships with colleagues and coworkers.

    It has been revealed that work on being clear and concise in emails, meetings, and in conversations. Practicing good communication not only improves your productivity but also helps avoid misunderstandings (these 13 tips can help).

    If you’re overwhelmed and juggling too much, look for tasks that can be given to others to make your life easier. This doesn’t mean you’re not good at your job. It just means you're making sure your energy is spent where it’s needed most.

    It has been revealed that struggling to focus? Single-tasting is where it’s at. Take on one task at a time and not five at once. This will improve the quality of your work and help you feel less like you want to scream.

    Recent findings suggest that even if it’s scary, seek out feedback from your boss, coworkers, or clients. Constructive input can help you get better and show that you want to improve. Just make sure you’re also receiving feedback for things you’re doing well, not just areas where you could do better.

    Find a method that helps you stay on top of deadlines. A to-do list app, a daily planner, or a bullet journal could help keep track of all your tasks. Explore some different ideas to find what works best for you.

    Don’t hesitate to ask for what you need. If anything, this can help you get taken more seriously and help with career growth. Ask for that raise, request that more flexible schedule, tell your boss you need additional resources to complete that project.

    💙 Learn how to practice Speaking Up at work with this session from the Mindful Leadership Wisdom Series.

    Set goals that align with your long-term dreams and values, not just what you hope to achieve. These could be around building confidence, becoming a more mindful leader, or exploring a newly introduced field you’ve always been interested in.

    Industry observers note that when you don’t feel mentally like you’re firing on all cylinders, it can be tough to even think of what to focus on to help your mental health. We get it — you’re probably already stressed, so making a decision on a resolution to be less stressed might be the last thing you want to (or can) do.

    To help you out, we put together a list of 15 small and intentional resolutions that will help nurture your mind and create space for calm and joy in 2027.

    According to recent reports, (Psst: You don’t have to do all of them. Start with one or two that’ll help you feel more balanced, calm, and connected, and then go from there.).

    According to recent reports, write down and reflect on your thoughts, feelings, and experiences each day. This can help you process your emotions and recognize some patterns you have. Journaling is also a great way to practice gratitude.

    Industry observers note that each day, take a moment to think of three things you’re grateful for. This can rewire your brain to look for the positives in your life. It doesn’t have to be getting a promotion or finding your perfect partner, it can be as small as not burning your bagel today. If you want to find more ways to incorporate gratitude into your days, here are eight ideas to get you started.

    Spend a few minutes a day practicing mindfulness. And while this could be a five minute meditation, it could also be a bit of deep breathing on a work break, or just noticing the sights and sounds on your morning walk. Any moment where you become fully present counts!

    According to recent reports, go to bed and wake up at the same time every day to help you get better quality sleep (here are six more tips to help you get those Zzzzs). The more rested you are, the more you’ll be able to handle the stress that comes up throughout the day.

    According to recent reports, nature has a way of calming us down and recharging us, so if it’s possible, try to get outside everyday. It doesn't have to be a substantial hike, it can be as simple as walking around your block or even just going into your yard.

    This is a big one! Try to gradually reduce the time you spend on your phone, computer, or watching TV, especially before bed. You could read that novel that’s been on your bedside table for ever or catch up with a loved one instead. But take it slow, we know it’s not easy.

    Give yourself permission to say no to things that overwhelm or overcommit you. It’s more important to protect your energy than to burn yourself out trying to please other people. If saying no is hard for you, here’s 30 ways to do it nicely.

    According to recent reports, get in the habit of reaching out to a loved one or a therapist when you’re feeling stressed or overwhelmed. Talking about our feelings can help us feel lighter and even give us a new perspective.

    In a recent development, A clean environment isn’t just for your desk. Having a clean home can calm you too. So take some small steps to organize your home. You might try doing just one room at a time, it doesn’t need to be all at once.

    According to recent reports, schedule regular breaks so you don’t have a meltdown. These pauses can really help you reduce your stress and keep you focused. Grabbing a glass of water, breathing deeply, or gently stretching can all help reset you and give your mind a moment to rest.

    According to recent reports, treat yourself the way you would your closest friend. Avoid going in on yourself with harsh, critical thoughts and instead say some sweet nothings to yourself. We know this isn’t always easy, so here are eight tips to help you quiet that inner critic.

    Sources indicate that start a hobby that lets you express yourself. This can be therapeutic and put you in a better mood. Ever been curious about painting or playing music? Maybe now’s your chance to explore that curiosity.

    Exercising relieves a lot of stress. But you don’t need to spend hours at the gym or set some substantial weight loss goal. Instead, try out a new yoga class, have a dance party in your living room, or find other ways to move your body that feel nourishing to you.

    According to recent reports, go easy on yourself, you don’t need to be perfect (newsflash: there’s no such thing). It can help to focus on all the small ways you're growing each day, not on the destination. Sometimes it’s better to think about growth-setting instead of goal setting.

    Don’t regularly spend your time on something that drains your energy. Seek out places that bring you positivity instead. If certain people you hang around with make you feel bad, limit your exposure to them. This might look like setting boundaries with family about how many events you attend each year, or with friends by limiting how much you talk or get together.

    💙 If you’re looking for more positivity in your life, learn how to Process and Move Past Negativity during the Overcome Stress and Anxiety series with Dr. Julie Smith.

    Okay, let’s face it. Most of us want to look and feel our best — and there’s nothing wrong with that. But better physical health is also about feeling energized, staying strong, and giving our body the help it needs to thrive.

    According to recent reports, we don’t need to tell you that working out consistently is a lot easier said than done. Sure, in a perfect world, we always have the time and energy to get to the gym. But we don’t live in that world. We have endless responsibilities and working out might be the first thing to go when we’re busy.

    So explore these 15 manageable resolutions that can help you feel strong and energized going into 2027. And remember, you don’t need to force yourself to go all-in on physical wellness to feel better. Just start with one or two that feel like they’d be easier to make a consistent habit and go from there.

    According to recent reports, aim for some form of movement every day –– it doesn’t have to be intense. Try a 10–minute stretch or a brisk walk through your favorite part of your neighborhood. Focus on what makes you feel good in your body, which may change day to day.

    Recent findings suggest that hydration makes you feel good and stay alert, so try to aim for 8–10 glasses of water a day. Carry a reusable water bottle with you to make it easier to hit your goal and remind you to drink. If regular water feels boring try adding slices of your favorite citrus or fresh mint to your water.

    Add a rainbow of foods to your plate! Focus on eating a mix of fruits, veggies, lean proteins, and whole grains. Try meal prepping ahead of time to make it easier for you to choose healthy options. Bonus points if you try to stay mindful while you cook and while you eat — here’s how.

    Swap out processed snacks for healthier options like fruit, nuts, seeds, or yogurt. Try keeping nutritious snacks nearby to make it easier to avoid reaching your favorite sweets. With that in mind, don’t forget that dark chocolate has some antioxidants so adding a few dark chocolate chips to your trail mix is a-okay with us!

    When you sleep better, you feel better. End of story. Aim for around eight hours of quality sleep each night. It can help to have a wind down routine at the end of your day to help your body know that it’s time for rest. These nine steps can help you create a calming bedtime routine.

    In a recent development, if you are able to take stairs instead of elevators or escalators, go for it! Making small, active choices throughout your day to help you get a little more movement. You could also try parking farther away to get in a few extra steps.

    Recent findings suggest that add some stretching into your daily routine to improve your flexibility, reduce your tension, and prevent injuring yourself. Try stretching for a few minutes as soon as you get out of bed or right before you get into bed — here are seven we like.

    We know it can be frustrating or scary to go see a doctor, but don’t wait to see one until you feel sick. Set up your physicals and dental cleanings so that you can breathe easy and not worry about your health. You’ll be proud of yourself when you leave that doctor’s office!

    Generally, it’s recommended to cut back on foods high in sugar. You may be surprised how much sugar some of your daily go-tos have, so stay mindful of what you’re consuming (you could check the labels for sugar content if that works for you).. It’s not about never having a treat, but bringing more awareness to what you’re eating and how it’s making you feel. It’s all about balance.

    Sources indicate that working out can really feel like work a lot of the time. So shake up your routine to help keep you excited to exercise. Ever tried kickboxing or swimming? Maybe 2027 is the year you hop in the boxing ring or jump in the pool.

    If you have a desk job, try to stand up and move every hour. Consider switching to a standing desk if that’s an option. If you work from home and have space for a walking pad in front of a standing desk you can also get your steps in while you work.

    It has been revealed that we know that the upcoming year isn’t always the time you want to get outside for a walk, but sunshine and time in nature can boost your mood. If you live in the northern hemisphere, bundle up and try going for a walk, run, or bike ride outside whenever the weather allows it.

    If you drink alcohol, consider cutting back by a few drinks or setting limits. It can help to have fun or festive swap, so try sipping on flavored sparkling water or a mocktail at a social event or as a treat at the end of a long week. Sometimes creating a special drink that’s free of booze creates the same excitement as making a special cocktail. And you might love the way you feel the next morning when you’re hydrating your body with your evening beverage instead of dehydrating it.

    According to recent reports, good posture helps prevent back and neck pain so pay attention to how you sit and stand. And add exercises that focus on strengthening your core into your workout. This will help support better alignment. Sitting at a desk for work? Set alarms every so often to remind you to stand up and stretch.

    Sources indicate that celebrating your progress helps you to keep going — we all need a good pat on the back. If you drink an extra glass of water or walk an extra mile, take note of it. Maybe even do a little happy dance. If you go for a walk four days in a row, make a note in your journal or notebook. The more you celebrate your progress the prouder of yourself you’ll be (and the easier it is to keep it up).

    💙 Learn how to celebrate the Small Wins on the path to achieving your larger goals with help from Jay Shetty.

    Fresh Year’s resolutions are personal goals or promises you make to yourself at the start of a new year. They can be about anything and it’s entirely up to you. They can be big like training for a marathon or small like drinking more water.

    In a recent development, usually people use it as a chance to reflect, change up some patterns in their life, and start fresh. If you’re looking to set a resolution but don’t know where to start, here are five areas people tend to focus on:.

    You don’t have to make resolutions to have a wonderful upcoming year. But if you want to try, keep in mind that resolutions work best when you make them work for you. So yes — resolutions matter if you use them as a tool to help you live with more purpose and joy, then you’ll set yourself up for more success.

    Recent findings suggest that when you’re setting your resolutions, focus on what would make you feel happier, healthier and more fulfilled and go from there. And approach resolutions with kindness and flexibility, especially if you don’t end up following through on one.

    Industry observers note that if the idea of resolutions feels overwhelming — we get it. Here’s three ways that could make it easier for you:.

    Focus on one word or theme for the year that feels right to you, like “balance” or “growth.”.

    Set a small monthly intention instead of a year-long commitment.

    Celebrate progress instead of perfection by noticing little wins along the way.

    We wish there were five magical resolutions that could solve all of our problems at once. But unfortunately there’s no such thing. What we can tell you is the most successful resolutions tend to be the ones that feel right to you.

    In a recent development, it’s important to focus on the right area when setting your resolution, so you’ll be more likely to stick with them. Here are five areas to focus on when setting your resolution:.

    Resolutions that focus on building stronger relationships — Pick ones that’ll fill you up and add more joy to your life.

    Resolutions that focus on taking care of your physical health — Pick ones that focus on regular exercise, better nutrition, or improved sleep.

    Resolutions that focus on your mental health — Pick ones that practice gratitude or mindfulness, so that they can help you feel calmer and more balanced.

    Resolutions that focus on your career –– Pick ones that focus on learning a latest skill or creating a better work-life balance so that your professional life can become more rewarding.

    Resolutions that focus on personal growth –– Pick ones that focus on starting upcoming hobbies or giving back to your community.

    Industry observers note that all of us at one point or another have probably failed at a resolution we’ve set for ourselves. And when that happens, it can feel pretty disappointing. But resolutions can work — if you set them in the right way.

    Resolutions that are vague or overly ambitious tend to be a recipe for failure. But if you set ones that are realistic and meaningful to you, it’ll be a lot easier to keep your resolution and see the change you want. But remember to be flexible and kind to yourself. We’re all not perfect and mistakes happen. So try not to beat yourself up if you don’t stick to your goals perfectly. Focus on progress, not perfection.

    Sources indicate that if you find it easier to set monthly intentions as opposed to setting one year-long resolution, go for that. Tailor the resolutions so they work best for you.

    Sometimes the minute we think of resolutions, we can get sad or overwhelmed at the baggage of our past failed resolutions. If this is you — we understand. Resolutions aren’t for everyone. But if you’re interested, there are other ways you can focus on self-improvement and growth.

    If a long list of goals is too daunting for you, try picking a single word to guide your year. You could use words like “balance,” or “connection,” to remind yourself to make choices that match with your values.

    If setting smaller, short-term goals might help you to stay motivated, you could try focusing on building better sleep habits in January, and then shifting to something like improving your diet in February.

    It has been revealed that if tracking your progress will make it more fun for you and help you to invest more, try using a habit tracker app, or even just a calendar. This way it’ll be easier to celebrate your little wins along the way.

    Resolutions that focus on relationships can bring more connection, understanding, and happiness into your life. And a good way to show the people you love the most how much they mean to you is to set a resolution to spend more quality time with them.

    Sources indicate that acts of kindness also go a long way to strengthen your relationships. So if this is vital to you, try setting an intention to express gratitude more often, like thanking your partner for their support.

    You could also set a resolution to unplug more often. This can help free up your time and create more meaningful, distraction-free moments with the people you care about the most.

    Tech Report: How Kindness Unlocks Happiness In Our Brains

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Small acts of kindness and self-compassion can interrupt a cycle of self-criticism and release neurotransmitters that create a sense of wellbeing.
    • Some years ago, my daughter was beaten up at a kids’ gathering.
    • In the World Happiness Report, researchers looked at kindness as a factor contributing to happiness, and they developed a novel way to study the prevalence of kind acts.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Small acts of kindness and self-compassion can interrupt a cycle of self-criticism and release neurotransmitters that create a sense of wellbeing.

    Some years ago, my daughter was beaten up at a kids’ gathering. I asked myself as a psychologist, “What happened to kindness? When did we lose it?”.

    I started to dig into the research. In the World Happiness Report, researchers looked at kindness as a factor contributing to happiness, and they developed a novel way to study the prevalence of kind acts. They tracked “lost” wallets to see if they were returned. They found that more people were helping strangers than was reported before the pandemic, which may be surprising.

    Recent findings suggest that other social science studies found that measurably happier people live in areas where community members tend to donate more, volunteer their time, or help strangers. In other words, helping inspires more helping.

    [Download: Get a Grip on Tough Emotions].

    What explains this kindness-happiness connection? In short, giving or receiving kindness kickstarts a “helper’s high” in our brains.

    Research reveals that acts of kindness engage certain brain networks that release good chemicals like an internal pharmacy:.

    Recent findings suggest that the dopamine from a helper’s high is different from the endorphin hit associated with running, gaming, or gambling, which keeps you wanting more. The dopamine generated in a helper’s high continues to produce positive feelings over time. The release of these neurotransmitters is especially helpful for people with ADHD who may struggle with emotional control, motivation, and stress.

    Recent findings suggest that studies have shown that volunteering, even for one hour a week, can reduce inflammatory and stress cortisol responses, and even increase longevity. Volunteering is also considered a preventative action for loneliness and depression. Teens who volunteer outside their homes are more resilient and less likely to become depressed, according to research.

    Helping people learn to be kind to themselves is my lifelong challenge as a clinical psychologist. We tend to prioritize other people’s needs over our own. But the research is clear on self-compassion: When you talk to yourself in a kinder way, or do kind things for yourself, you’re learning how to quiet that inner critic.

    [Read: Self-Compassion: The Newly introduced ADHD Treatment].

    Here are five practices to improve your self-compassion.

    Tara Cousineau, Ph.D., is a clinical psychologist, meditation teacher, and self-described recovering perfectionist. She is the author of The Kindness Cure and The Perfectionist’s Dilemma.

    Tech Report: Growing Older on the Spectrum: The Unique Needs of Autistic Adults

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (887 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Additudemag

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Because so few studies focus on aging in autistic adults, there is little understanding—and support—for the specialized needs they may have later in life.
    • It has been revealed that our understanding of autism has evolved considerably over the last 50 years.
    • According to recent reports, but even as our understanding has grown, we still know very little about the unique needs and challenges of autistic people in midlife and beyond, or about the supports that help most.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Because so few studies focus on aging in autistic adults, there is little understanding—and support—for the specialized needs they may have later in life.

    It has been revealed that our understanding of autism has evolved considerably over the last 50 years. Today, many autistic adults who were overlooked or misdiagnosed in childhood are finally pursuing a proper evaluation and diagnosis.

    According to recent reports, but even as our understanding has grown, we still know very little about the unique needs and challenges of autistic people in midlife and beyond, or about the supports that help most. Why? Because less than 1 percent of all indexed autism research has focused on midlife and older age.

    In a recent development, that means we still don’t understand the cognitive, health, and social experiences of autistic adults as they age. And this lack of research influences clinical practice: Historically, clinicians haven’t been trained and equipped with an understanding of autism in older age.

    An analysis of health records from the United Kingdom indicates that around 90 percent of autistic people in midlife (ages 40 to 59), and 96 percent of older adults (ages 60 and beyond), are undiagnosed.1 Until autism research and diagnosis rates improve, we won’t understand the full autistic experience, but here are the truths coming into focus.

    [Read: “How Can I Get Evaluated for Autism as an Adult?”].

    Autism in older age is associated with complex health needs. Compared with the general population, middle-aged and older autistic adults have higher rates of several physical and mental health conditions, making frequent and proactive screenings key for this group.

    Industry observers note that despite the higher rates of dementia, Parkinson’s disease, and cognitive difficulties found among autistic adults, we should not assume that autism is linked to accelerated cognitive aging. Autistic people are no more likely to experience rapid cognitive aging than are members of the general population, according to research.

    However, one study found that about 20 percent of autistic people had highly variable cognitive profiles; this subgroup developed an old-age profile earlier than expected compared to non-autistic adults. For these individuals, red flags for cognitive decline and dementia may present at a younger age than we’d expect in the general population. Autistic adults who fit this profile may require additional help and support as they age to remain safe and independent.

    Sleep typically deteriorates with age, however, adults with high autistic traits are more likely than others to report moderate or severe sleep problems as they grow older, including problems with falling and staying asleep, sleep efficiency, and daytime tiredness.

    Recent findings suggest that sleep is a lynchpin for general and mental health. Sleep problems, for example, tend to worsen anxiety, a condition that is highly prevalent among autistic adults. Improving sleep quality by blocking out light with curtains, using earplugs or a white noise machine, choosing pajamas and bedsheets made from soothing fabrics, and/or using a weighted blanket can significantly benefit the mental health of autistic people as they age.

    [Read: This is Why You’re Always Tired].

    Sources indicate that sensory processing differences are part of the autistic experience. Over a lifetime, exposure to difficult and unpleasant sensory experiences, like crowded, noisy environments, is linked to mental health problems in older autistic adults. At the same time, even small changes, such as noise-canceling headphones or wearing a face mask in public, can help. Adjustments and accommodations such as these should not be overlooked when thinking of health and quality of life.

    Sources indicate that compared with non-autistic people, autistic adults experience higher rates of loneliness — the subjective feeling of lacking meaningful connection. While middle-aged and older autistic people tend to have small social networks, about one in five autistic adults has no contact with family or friends in a given month, compared with one in 20 neurotypical adults. Certain neurodivergent traits — rigidity, flat affect or an aloof personality, and communication challenges — may help explain social difficulties.

    Interestingly, in the general population, we found that women tend to be lonelier than men. In the autistic population, the feeling of loneliness was more common in men.

    Industry observers note that connections with family and friends seem to provide a protective mental health benefit and lead to a better quality of life. Supporting autistic people in forming meaningful relationships on their own terms and in relation to their passions and interests could be a key target for interventions.

    Best meditation apps of 2027 and how to choose the right one

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • You open the app store to look for a meditation app and find dozens of options promising calmer days, deeper sleep, less stress, and sharper focus.
    • It has been revealed that below, we cover three well-known meditation apps: Calm, Headspace, and Insight Timer.
    • Before we dive in, a quick note on where we’re coming from.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    You open the app store to look for a meditation app and find dozens of options promising calmer days, deeper sleep, less stress, and sharper focus. It’s hard to know where to start or which claims to believe.

    It has been revealed that below, we cover three well-known meditation apps: Calm, Headspace, and Insight Timer. We've looked at what each one offers and named what we like about it, so you can decide which one to try.

    Before we dive in, a quick note on where we’re coming from. We make Calm, and we love it. We hope you will too, but another option might suit you better.

    It has been revealed that the best meditation app for you depends on what you’re looking for. To narrow it down, ask yourself these questions:.

    It has been revealed that what do you want help with? Maybe it’s stress relief, better sleep, sharper focus, or a guided start as a beginner.

    How much variety do you need? Some people want an extensive library to explore, while others prefer a smaller collection built around a specific goal.

    How personal do you want it to feel? You might prefer an app that tailors recommendations to your mood and goals, or one that leaves the choosing to you.

    Recent findings suggest that what's your budget? Compare what the free and paid tiers include, since a generous free version may be all you need.

    Calm is one of the most widely used meditation apps, and it also offers sleep content, music, gentle movement sessions, and more. People use Calm at night for sleep and during the day for stress.

    Content library: The app features Sleep Stories, bedtime tales read by well-known voices, alongside daily meditation programs including the flagship Daily Calm. You'll also find breathwork exercises, mindful tools, soundscapes, intro courses, and longer programs on themes like anxiety and self-kindness.

    Personalization: Calm’s Check-Ins let you log your mood, sleep, and gratitude, so you can spot patterns over time. You can set reminders and follow a series of sessions to build a routine.

    In a recent development, standout feature: For us, it's the sleep content. Sleep Stories are the first thing we’d recommend to a friend who’s struggling with sleep.

    Headspace is another widely-used meditation app, and it leans into teaching. Many sessions are organized into courses that walk you through a topic step by step.

    Recent findings suggest that content library: The app features beginner courses and SOS meditations, short sessions for when stress spikes. It also has themed collections for focus and movement. For sleep, there are Sleepcasts.

    Personalization: Headspace offers personalized recommendations and its AI companion, Ebb, lets you talk through how you’re feeling and suggests app content in response.

    Standout feature: We like how Headspace gives beginners a clear path to follow, starting with its 10-session Basics course.

    Insight Timer started as a meditation timer and grew into a large library of guided meditations, with plenty of free content and a paid tier called MemberPlus.

    Content library: The app hosts a catalog of meditations, talks, and music tracks, plus a meditation timer for people who prefer to sit in silence.

    Personalization: You can join teacher-led challenges to help you stay on track, and the streak feature tracks how many days in a row you’ve meditated.

    Industry observers note that standout feature: We like how much the app offers for free. With so much available, you can try a range of teachers before paying for anything.

    In a recent development, calm won’t be right for everyone, but here’s why we love it. (Keep in mind that this section is our point of view, not a neutral comparison.).

    Recent findings suggest that the daily meditations are a great place to start. There are three to choose from, and each has its own feel:.

    The Daily Calm, with Tamara Levitt, leans toward gentle reflection.

    The Daily Jay, with Jay Shetty, draws on psychology and timeless wisdom.

    The Daily Trip, with Jeff Warren, suits curious meditators who like to experiment.

    Sources indicate that you may click with one voice more than the others, so it’s worth trying all three to find out whether you’re a Tamara, Jay, or Jeff person. (There’s a fourth daily too, the Daily Move, a short mindful movement session — a great way to get your body ready for the day.).

    Sources indicate that we’ve also produced a lot of quick meditations over the past few years, all under five minutes. So even the busiest person, or the most skeptical first-timer, has something small to try.

    Sources indicate that sleep is the other main reason we keep coming back. With our Sleep Stories and nighttime meditations, we’ve unlocked a delightful way to let go of the worries of the day, relax your mind and body, and allow yourself to fall (and stay) asleep easily and naturally. Our 500+ Sleep Stories include some of the world’s most celebrated and soothing voices, like Harry Styles, Cynthia Erivo, Idris Elba, Rosé, and Greta Lee. With plenty more to choose from, there’s always something fresh to help you wind down and drift off.

    Industry observers note that then there’s how the app looks and feels. The visuals lean into calming nature—think misty forests, rain on a window, slow ocean waves—so opening the app itself sets the scene for calm. And if you just need to tune out the world for a while, our Rain on Leaves soundscape is a legit vibe.

    According to recent reports, the numbers back up the impact. More than 180 million people worldwide have downloaded Calm, and its content has been studied in peer-reviewed research. For example, in one randomized trial of 88 stressed college students, those who used Calm for eight weeks reported lower perceived stress than a wait-list group.

    It has been revealed that they may help, though the research is still young. An updated review of 45 randomized trials found improvements in anxiety and depression symptoms among people using mindfulness apps, compared with control groups. The effects were modest, and the authors note we still need larger, higher-quality studies to say how much apps help and for whom.

    It has been revealed that an app also isn’t a substitute for professional care. If you’re struggling with your mental health, it’s worth talking to a doctor, who can help you find the right support.

    Related read: The science behind Calm: 27 studies and surveys.

    It has been revealed that yes, though how much is free varies a lot. Calm and Headspace each offer a limited selection of free sessions plus a free trial of their paid prepares, with most of the library behind a subscription. Insight Timer works the other way around: the bulk of its catalog is free, with a paid MemberPlus tier for extras like courses and offline listening.

    To choose the right meditation app, start with your main goal, whether that’s stress relief, better sleep, or a guided start as a beginner. From there, check prices and any features you care about, like offline listening or language options. Then take advantage of the free trials. Most apps offer one, and it’s a good way to see how an app fits before you pay. While you’re trying it out, sample a few different narrators. A lot of meditation comes down to the voice guiding you, and finding someone you connect with can turn the practice into something you look forward to.

    It has been revealed that calm is worth it if you want to ease stress and anxiety, sleep better, focus when your mind wanders, or learn the basics of meditation. The app may be a helpful way to build a daily mental health habit, with support for moments from a racing mind at bedtime to a hard day at work. Whether you need quick relief in the moment or ongoing support through a life change, Calm is for you.

    You can try a 7-day free trial to see how it fits your flow, and you don’t need to know which content format you prefer ahead of time.

    Calm and Headspace have a lot in common. Both offer guided meditation, beginner-friendly courses, short sessions for when stress spikes, sleep content, and mindful movement. The difference is in the mix and the overall feel. On Calm, you’ll find hundreds of Sleep Stories read by well-known voices, daily meditations from a rotating cast of instructors, music, soundscapes, and Emergency Calm sessions for high-stress moments. On Headspace, you’ll find a more course-led, step-by-step approach and an AI companion called Ebb. Both offer free content and a free trial, so the best way to decide is to try each and see which feels right for you.

    Mental health is hard. Getting support doesn't have to be. The Calm app puts the tools to feel better in your back pocket, with personalized content to manage stress and anxiety, get better sleep, and feel more present in your life.

    According to recent reports, neurodivergent kids aren’t the only ones who struggle with changing routines or new life phases. Adults can feel overwhelmed by transitions, too.

    Whether starting a upcoming job, moving to a new town, or sending a child off to college, transitions are equal parts exciting and uncomfortable for neurodivergent individuals.

    The struggle often looks different in children and adults, but the demand is much the same: Stop what you are doing, shift your attention, figure out the next step, manage your emotions, and move into a different role, task, place, or expectation. The bigger the transition, the harder it feels.

    Typical transitions include returning to work after a vacation, adjusting to a new schedule, shifting from work to parenting mode, navigating relationship changes, and recovering from illness or injury.

    [Free Download: Get Control of Your Life and Schedule].

    Recent findings suggest that from the outside, the response of an adult with ADHD may look like procrastination, avoidance, irritability, disorganization, or poor follow-through. Internally, they are likely dealing with anxiety, emotional overload, decision fatigue, time blindness, or the frustration of knowing exactly what needs to be done but struggling to begin.

    “I struggle so badly with transitions (they feel almost literally painful) that I spend up to five hours in a state of crippling inertia before handling a task that needs to be done,” wrote one woman with ADHD in a social media post, pleading for help.

    It has been revealed that transitions can be especially difficult when they involve uncertainty. A fresh job may bring excitement and anxiety about performance. A vacation may feel adventurous and overwhelming. Even a positive life change can feel unsettling when structure falls away.

    “I don’t travel much,” indicates Layla, an ADDitude reader from California. “Transitions are hard for me.”.

    [Get This Free Download: Finish Your To-Do List Today].

    According to recent reports, most importantly, adults with ADHD should keep in mind that embracing change easily is not necessarily a sign of maturity. Feelings of anxiety around transitions may just mean that your brain needs more preview, structure, recovery, and support to move from one demand to the next.

    What Couples Married For 40 Years Do When Life Gets Hard

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Couples married for decades reveal what they turned to when they thought their marriage might end.
    • Couples married for decades reveal what they turned to when they thought their marriage might end.
    • When people in decades-long marriages describe what helped them through a crisis, most of the responses they give involve leaning on each other.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Couples married for decades reveal what they turned to when they thought their marriage might end.

    Couples married for decades reveal what they turned to when they thought their marriage might end.

    When people in decades-long marriages describe what helped them through a crisis, most of the responses they give involve leaning on each other.

    They describe listening to each other, talking through painful subjects and sometimes having the same argument more than once.

    The researchers suggest that this response grows out of years of knowing they can count on their partner.

    In attachment theory, a partner can act as a safe haven, someone whose presence makes it easier to bear distress.

    Getting through a difficult period together may deepen that trust, making it easier to ask for help the next time it is needed.

    Dr Christian Heim, the study’s first author, and Dr Caroline Heim, study co-author, interviewed each couple together, asking each person to describe what had put their marriage under strain and what had helped them cope.

    The 180 participants were born in 24 countries and, with a few exceptions, had been married for at least 40 years.

    Around two-thirds of the couples described a threat they believed could have ended their marriage, such as the death or serious illness of a child, infidelity or prolonged periods apart.

    Talking, listening and arguing accounted for almost a quarter of the coping responses the researchers recorded.

    After an affair, some couples described arguing over it repeatedly, while bereaved partners sometimes waited for a moment when both felt able to speak.

    One partner in an American couple married for 45 years recalled asking their spouse about the son they had lost.

    Recent findings suggest that “Can I talk about our son? I’m hurting. Is it okay to talk about it?”.

    Some partners described taking time to grieve separately before they were ready to turn to each other.

    Around four in five coping responses involved leaning on the relationship, whether by drawing closer, persevering as a couple or giving up something one partner wanted.

    The interviews capture what couples in lasting marriages felt had helped them, leaving open whether the same approaches would have helped couples who separated.

    When partners see a problem as something they face together, they may spend less time working out who is to blame and more time trying to understand what the other person is going through.

    A previous analysis involving almost 18,000 people found that coping together and helping a partner manage stress were both linked to greater relationship satisfaction (Falconier et al., 2015).

    Some couples in the interviews felt that an illness, a bereavement or a family conflict had left them closer, even though the experience itself had been painful.

    A British couple married for 60 years described how they got through a serious conflict with their in-laws:.

    The study was published in the journal The American Journal of Family Therapy (Heim & Heim, 2025).

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    When we add another bolognese to the blog (Yes, we already have versions 1, 2, 3, and 4), you know it’s something special! This newest version is made with EGGPLANT, meaning it’s the perfect bolognese for late summer. It’s light yet satisfying, creamy yet bright, and full of bold Italian-inspired flavor — everyone will be asking for seconds!

    It has been revealed that even better? It’s a breeze to make — just 1 pot required! What are you waiting for? Get that pasta water boiling!

    Bolognese is an Italian sauce that gets its name from the Italian city of Bologna. It’s typically made with meat, soffrito (onions, celery, and carrots), white wine, milk, and tomato paste or sauce, all simmered to create a rich, flavorful sauce.

    Our eggplant version strays from the traditional as it excludes meat (and includes eggplant) and incorporates dairy alternatives. But the rest of the dish is very similar to traditional bolognese and feels so hearty it might convert even the most adamant veggie skeptics!

    According to recent reports, this 1-pot eggplant bolognese is everything you want for a cozy pasta night, minus the fuss! It starts with sautéing onion and carrots to create a simple, savory-sweet base. Next, we add eggplant (cut into very small cubes) and let it sauté until it has softened and browned (hello, flavor!).

    Sources indicate that build the flavor even further with garlic and red pepper flakes and by deglazing the pan with wine. Crushed tomatoes and tomato paste ensure a bright, tomato-forward sauce, and a small amount of dairy-free milk (we like homemade cashew milk) gives it a gentle creaminess and richness. The final flavor touches include dried Italian herbs (basil + oregano), sea salt, and maple syrup to balance the acidity of the tomatoes.

    Once all the ingredients are in your pan, it’s time to let the heat do its magic. Simmering for at least 20-30 minutes allows the sauce to thicken and concentrates the flavors as liquid evaporates away. If you have the time, you can let it continue simmering for up to an hour for even more flavor!

    When it’s done simmering, you’ll be left with an oh-so delicious, plant-powered sauce perfect for serving with your favorite pasta! It would also be lovely over polenta and is elevated by garnishing with fresh basil and our homemade vegan parmesan cheese.

    The best birthday message is one that’s honest, reflecting how you feel about the person. Whether it’s a thoughtful one-liner or a whole paragraph, what matters most is that it sounds like you and is from the heart.

    To start writing a thoughtful birthday wish, think about what this person brings to your life. Are they the person who makes you laugh when things get heavy? Do they show up when others flake? Start there, and be as specific as possible.

    According to recent reports, you could even include a shared memory, a personal trait you admire, or something they’ve done recently that made you proud. It doesn’t matter if it’s short or long — just that it’s real and meaningful to you.

    If you don't know the person well, start your message by being warm and casual. Something like, “Wishing you a joyful day and a year filled with good things” works perfectly.

    If it’s for someone you know in a professional context, try, “Hope your day is filled with appreciation and celebration — you deserve it.”.

    You don’t have to fake closeness, but you can absolutely show care.

    It has been revealed that this one depends on your relationship with the person. If humor is a shared language between the two of you, you absolutely can. Just pay attention to the tone.

    Inside jokes, light teasing, or self-deprecating lines can be great, but if you’re unsure how your humor might be perceived, it’s safer to aim for warmth with a side of personality. Don’t try it if it starts feeling forced.

    Sources indicate that let’s be honest. “Happy birthday” gets the job done, but it’s also one of the most basic options. If you want to switch it up, try something a little more personal or playful.

    “Celebrating the fact that you exist today!”.

    According to recent reports, “Another year of you being excellent. Carry on.”.

    “Hope today treats you like the royalty you are (with cake).”.

    “Wishing you all the good stuff, and no fine print.”.

    Recent findings suggest that you can write a short, warm note that fits how well you know the person. One or two sentences is plenty.

    If you’re close, an inside joke can work. If you’re not, thank them for something specific, like their help on a project or the way they greet everyone in the morning. For example, “Happy birthday, Priya. Thank you for always making time to help.”.

    It’s usually best to skip jokes about age or appearance, especially in a card other people will read. If a group card is going around, add your name and one line of your own instead of repeating what’s already written.

    Industry observers note that A short, sincere happy birthday message is one or two sentences that greet the person and share one kind thought. It doesn’t need a joke or a long story to mean something (and it works the same way in a text, a card, or on social media).

    Recent findings suggest that A basic format is the person’s name, “happy birthday,” and one line about them or your hopes for their year. For example, “Happy birthday, Maya. I’m so glad you’re in my life.” Or, “Happy birthday, Dan. Hope this year brings you more rest and more cake.”.

    It has been revealed that my daughter got sick last week, which means that our whole family got sick last week. And when I get sick, I lose two things: 1) my appetite, and 2) my interest in cooking.

    It has been revealed that this pastina soup truly SAVED us last week. It is:.

    It has been revealed that I can’t say enough about how much I loved this last week. I sat down at the table with a steamy bowl with extra parm on top, and found myself repeatedly going back for “just one more scoop” of the broth over those tiny stars, even though I swore I hadn’t been feeling hungry just a moment earlier.

    My girls were pretty excited about eating tiny star pasta with olive oil + Parmesan, while Bjork and I ladled the luscious broth over our bowls and finally tucked into some nurturing food for the first time in several days.

    Pastina refers to the tiny star shaped pasta, which I found at Target, and the nickname Italian Penicillin refers to the healing nature of the savory broth – almost like a chicken noodle soup, but simpler. (And if I’m being honest, I prefer this to chicken noodle.).

    Sources indicate that I hope you are healthy and well, physically and emotionally. But if you’re not, this is comfort meal that has been serving our family so well lately!

    I keep them real chunky, and I give them a quick sauté with olive oil before adding all the liquid just to get things extra fragrant.

    I use water and Better Than Bouillon broth base.

    Transfer to a bowl to cool down for a moment.

    And then add them right back to the broth pot.

    Source Notes: “Italian penicillin” is a nickname for pastina soup, or pastina (small pasta) in broth. It is playfully compared to medicine because of its healing vibe, being that it is a warm, nostalgic, nourishing comfort food. It originated with generations of Italian grandmothers and it has moved into the spotlight after becoming a popular trend on TikTok over the last few years. 🙂.

    It has been revealed that this soup has become my go-to recipe when my family is sick. The broth is amazing – simple, light, flavorful, and nourishing! It’s absolute comfort food.

    Cheesy Vegan Enchilada Skillet (30 Minutes!)

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, everything you love about enchiladas, minus the fuss!
    • Recent findings suggest that this easy, nourishing dish features tender cubed sweet potato or winter squash, fiber- & protein-rich black beans, and a rich red enchilada sauce.
    • It has been revealed that it’s believed that enchiladas may have originated from a similar Mayan dish called papadzules.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, everything you love about enchiladas, minus the fuss! This super flavorful, cheesy vegan enchilada skillet comes together in about 30 minutes with simple methods, minimal dishes, and no need to fill or roll tortillas.

    Recent findings suggest that this easy, nourishing dish features tender cubed sweet potato or winter squash, fiber- & protein-rich black beans, and a rich red enchilada sauce. Everything gets simmered in 1 pan and topped with a melty cashew “cheese” that makes it SUPER satisfying and delicious!

    It has been revealed that it’s believed that enchiladas may have originated from a similar Mayan dish called papadzules. But the first written recipe for enchiladas was in an 1831 cookbook called El Cocinero mexicano. Typically, enchiladas are made with meat, seafood, beans, cheese, potatoes, or vegetables stuffed in corn tortillas and topped with enchilada sauce.

    Our “inspired-by” enchilada skillet has all the flavors of classic enchiladas, but it’s vegan, and instead of rolling the filling in tortillas, we slice the tortillas and cook everything together in one pan on the stovetop!

    Industry observers note that this 1-pan, 30-minute vegan enchilada skillet begins with a base of sautéed vegetables — onion, garlic, sweet potato, and poblano pepper. The veggies are flexible here, so feel free to experiment! We love kabocha squash for a fall variation and have found green bell peppers work well when poblanos aren’t available. We also think butternut squash would be nice, as would greens such as kale or spinach.

    Once the onions are very tender and the squash and peppers are just beginning to soften, we stir in black beans + corn tortillas that have been sliced into strips.

    In a recent development, next comes the final ingredient in the skillet portion of this dish (hello, simple + flavorful!): red enchilada sauce. We love the bold flavor of our homemade enchilada sauce (and usually have it stocked in the freezer), but this recipe also works well with store-bought enchilada sauce.

    Recent findings suggest that and lastly, it just wouldn’t be enchiladas without: the CHEESE! More specifically, a flavorful cashew “cheese” sauce inspired by our fan favorite Cheesy Vegan Pizza Beans. It’s made by blending up cashews, water, lime juice, garlic, tapioca starch, and sea salt. When poured over the enchilada skillet and covered with a lid, the heat and tapioca starch do their magic, creating a melty, cheesy layer! Total swoon!

    We highly recommend trying the cashew “cheese” sauce, even if you’re not vegan or dairy-free! It’s super easy and takes this dish to a whole fresh level. However, this enchilada skillet is also delicious with shredded vegan or dairy cheese (such as pepper jack).

    Sources indicate that we think you’ll LOVE this recipe! It’s:SmokySpicySuper flavorfulSatisfyingVersatileQuick & easy to make& SO delicious!

    This dish is hearty and amazing as a standalone quick meal for weeknights! It would also pair well with our Smoky Shredded Tofu Taco “Meat” or 1-Pan Mexican Shredded Chicken for a higher-protein option. Or, for more veggies, try it with our Crunchy Jicama Slaw or Quick Citrusy Cabbage Slaw.

    If you try this recipe, let us know! Leave a comment, rate it, and don’t forget to tag a photo @minimalistbaker on Instagram. Cheers, friends!

    ADHD in Midlife & Beyond: 5 Massive Research Findings

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (598 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Additudemag

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • “What helped someone with ADHD in their 20s is necessarily going to help them in their 60s, 70s, and 80s.”.
    • The experience of ADHD in midlife and older age is largely undocumented but not unimportant.
    • An estimated 66% of adults with ADHD ages 45 to 54 have no recorded diagnosis, according to an analysis of UK health records.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    “What helped someone with ADHD in their 20s is necessarily going to help them in their 60s, 70s, and 80s.”.

    The experience of ADHD in midlife and older age is largely undocumented but not unimportant.

    An estimated 66% of adults with ADHD ages 45 to 54 have no recorded diagnosis, according to an analysis of UK health records. Missed diagnoses and misdiagnoses make research on this population difficult — but not impossible.

    Amber John, Ph.D., a researcher at the University of Liverpool, reviewed studies on how the experience of ADHD changes with age during her November 2026 ADDitude webinar, “Aging with ADHD: Fresh Research Findings in Midlife and Beyond.”.

    Below are some of the themes John highlighted and what they suggest about the support adults with ADHD need in midlife and beyond.

    It has been revealed that in clinical interviews, adults with ADHD recalled feeling different growing up but being unable to explain why. A diagnosis helped them see those experiences in a different light.

    “These experiences that previously might have seemed disconnected, for many, started to form this more understandable pattern,” John mentioned. “And that could really change the meaning that someone gives to those past experiences, particularly where they had just been viewed as evidence of personal failings.”.

    [Read: The Transformative Power of an ADHD Diagnosis for Older Women].

    It has been revealed that many people with ADHD develop painstaking routines and coping strategies to manage symptoms. The effort it takes to keep those routines going often goes unseen and can fuel burnout.

    It has been revealed that “This raises a really important question about what it is that we actually mean when we say someone is functioning well,” John noted. “Understanding someone’s support needs really means that we need to ask about the cost of managing.”.

    In a recent development, the experience of ADHD changes as life circumstances change. Menopause, caring for aging parents, and retirement can affect how symptoms play out in daily life and disrupt routines that have helped people cope for decades.

    “A way that somebody is using to manage or to cope that’s worked in one period of life might become less useful when health, or demands, or available support changes,” John mentioned.

    Industry observers note that [Read: I Feared I Had Alzheimer’s. It Turns Out It Was Undiagnosed ADHD.].

    In doctors’ offices and workplaces, people with ADHD often shoulder the burden of explaining their needs and advocating for basic support. They can put considerable effort into managing their symptoms and still face barriers to getting care or participating at work.

    “There is a limit to focusing on individual-level coping because a person can put really substantial effort into managing whilst the environment actually continues to make participation difficult,” John mentioned.

    Industry observers note that john’s research highlights the need for ADHD support that adapts as people’s circumstances change. We shouldn’t assume that “what helped someone with ADHD in their 20s is necessarily going to help them in their 60s, 70s, and 80s,” she stated.

    For more on ADHD in midlife and beyond, watch the full webinar at additu.de/111726.

    #45991. How to spend Christmas alone (and actually enjoy it)

    How to spend Christmas alone (and actually enjoy it)

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1892 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Calm

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that it’s Christmas morning.
    • In a recent development, maybe you’re single, estranged or far from family, working the holiday, grieving, or just not in the mood to celebrate.
    • In fact, there are plenty of ways to make the day your own.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA.

    Industry observers note that it’s Christmas morning. The street outside is still, your phone hasn’t buzzed with plans, and the whole day is wide open, with no schedule and no one to check in with. It might feel like a relief, or it might ache. Sometimes it’s both in the same hour.

    In a recent development, maybe you’re single, estranged or far from family, working the holiday, grieving, or just not in the mood to celebrate. But no matter why you’re spending Christmas alone, the day can still feel warm and full.

    In fact, there are plenty of ways to make the day your own. Here you’ll find ideas for staying in or going out, plus what to do if it gets hard.

    Industry observers note that if you’re spending Christmas on your own, you’re far from the only one. More people live alone than ever, and plenty of people simply prefer a quiet holiday.

    Recent findings suggest that with that in mind, being alone and feeling lonely aren't the same thing. Being alone is a circumstance: no one else is around. Loneliness is a feeling of disconnection, and it can show up at a packed holiday table or an empty house.

    So what makes time alone feel good rather than lonely? A significant factor may be whether you have a say in how you spend it. In three studies where people reported on their moments throughout the day, time alone felt more positive when people chose it for themselves.

    In a recent development, if you didn’t choose to be alone this Christmas, it’s okay if that stings. What you do with the day is still up to you.

    Whether you’re in the mood for a slow day under a blanket, time out among people, or a bit of both, you don’t owe anyone an explanation for how you spend your day.

    Sources indicate that if you’re up for ideas, start here. If you’re feeling low, jump to How to deal with spending Christmas alone when hard feelings come up.

    If you’d rather stay in, here are a few ways to make the day at home feel comforting.

    Sources indicate that 1. Start the morning with meditation or journaling: Settle into a comfortable position and let your eyes close or soften. Tune into your breath and the sensations in your body. When thoughts about the day ahead drift in, notice them, then gently return to your breath. Journaling is another way to check in with how you’re feeling.

    Industry observers note that 💙 Want some guidance for those few minutes? Settle into the Mornings meditation on Calm.

    It has been revealed that 2. Cook or order the meal you really want: Skip the turkey-and-trimmings unless you love them. Go for whatever you're craving, whether that’s a roast for one, pancakes at noon, or your go-to takeout. Choosing food you’re excited about can turn an ordinary meal into a treat.

    💙 Listen to Piano for Rainy Days: Nice & Cozy while you cook.

    4. Do a movie marathon on your own terms: You get to choose what you watch, and no one talks through the good parts. Line up your favorite holiday films, or skip the Christmas theme entirely and binge the series you’ve been saving.

    According to recent reports, 5. Get lost in a book or an audiobook: A long, quiet day is a great chance to sink into a story without interruption. If your eyes get tired, switch to an audiobook while you putter around or lie on the couch.

    💙 Discover ten self-love activities to improve your well-being.

    If you’d like to spend the day out of the house, these ideas include solo outings and activities around other people. Holiday hours often change and volunteer spots fill up, so check details as early as you can..

    6. Spend time somewhere green: Stroll along a park path or trail, or find a bench and settle in for a while. Time in green space has been shown to quiet a busy mind. In one study, adults who walked for 90 minutes in nature reported less rumination (the looping, negative thinking that can feed low moods) than those who walked along a busy road.

    💙 Ready to step outside? Try Calm’s Nature Walk meditation with Dr. Eric López to soak in the sights, sounds, and smells around you.

    7. Volunteer for a few hours: Soup kitchens, shelters, and animal rescues often need extra hands on Christmas Day. Volunteering connects you with people who share a purpose, and research suggests performing acts of kindness may boost your well-being.

    💙 Feeling the urge to give back? Tune into the Random Acts of Kindness meditation on Calm to see how small gestures add up.

    Recent findings suggest that 8. Join a community meal or gathering: Many community centers and local groups host open Christmas meals. It’s a low-pressure way to share the day with others, even if only for a couple of hours.

    9. Find somewhere that’s open: Movie theaters, some cafés and restaurants, and hotel lounges often keep holiday hours. Even a little time around other people, strangers included, can bring a touch of connection to your day.

    According to recent reports, 10. Take a day trip: Head to a nearby town, hike a fresh trail, or visit a spot you’ve been meaning to see. A change of scenery can make the day feel like an occasion.

    There are many ways to make a quiet day feel less lonely, from a quick text to a mindfulness practice. Choose whichever of these appeal to you.

    Industry observers note that send a text, leave a voice note, or call someone you care about. If loved ones are far away, you could:.

    Schedule a call in advance, especially if you’re in different time zones.

    Do an activity together over video, like cooking or watching a movie.

    Ask for a family recipe, make it, and share how it turned out.

    You can start a tradition on your own. Keep it small and simple, such as a letter to your future self you open next year or a movie you rewatch every December 25.

    💙 Not sure where to start? Explore Redefining Traditions with therapist Kati Morton on Calm.

    Industry observers note that if you feel loneliness creeping in, a loving-kindness meditation may help you feel more connected. In one study, people who did a short loving-kindness meditation reported more feelings of social connection toward strangers than those who did a control task.

    💙 Press play on the Loving-Kindness meditation on Calm.

    Give yourself one thing to look forward to after your shift, such as a comfort meal or a call with someone you love. Treat yourself during the day with a good coffee or a walk on your break. You can also celebrate with others on another day, and it’s just as meaningful.

    💙 If you’re still feeling lonely after the holiday, here are seven tips to deal with loneliness.

    Recent findings suggest that even if you’ve chosen to be alone, Christmas can bring up emotions like sadness, envy, or grief. Here’s how to work through them.

    Recent findings suggest that other people’s picture-perfect holiday photos can leave you feeling like you’re missing out. Try stepping away from your phone for a few hours. Those posts are a highlight reel, and the rest of their day rarely looks as polished.

    It has been revealed that if the feeling lingers, try self-compassion: meeting yourself with the same warmth you’d offer a friend who’s feeling down. In a review of studies, people who practiced self-compassion reported lower anxiety, depression, and stress than people who didn’t. You could tell yourself, “This is hard, but I’m doing my best, and that’s enough.”.

    💙 Practice being a Friend on the Inside with Jeff Warren on Calm.

    If you’re missing someone this Christmas, the day can feel especially tender. You can honor them in subtle ways: cook their favorite dish, light a candle in their memory, or write them a letter. There’s no right way to grieve, so let the day be as quiet or as full as you need.

    Sources indicate that it’s okay to keep some distance from family on Christmas if you need to. Calls and replies are optional, and so is explaining your choice. You can mute the group chat for the day if that brings you some peace.

    If someone asks what you’re up to, you could say, “I’m keeping it low-key this year.” Whatever comes up, mixed feelings included, you don’t have to push it aside just because it’s the holidays.

    If your sadness lingers past the holiday, disrupts your sleep or appetite, or leaves you feeling hopeless, talk to a doctor or someone you trust. If you’re in the U.S. and need support right away, call or text 988 to reach the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. If you’re outside the U.S., findahelpline.com lists free local services.

    If you’re alone for Christmas, it can help to give the day some structure. Pick one or two things that excite you, such as a comfort meal, a long walk, or a movie, and let the rest of the day unfold naturally. A quick call or text with a loved one can be a nice touch, too.

    It has been revealed that it’s normal to want to spend Christmas alone. After a long or busy year, a quiet day can be restful, and preferring it doesn’t mean anything is wrong. Strategy the day around what appeals to you.

    Industry observers note that if you’d rather not stay home on Christmas, there are plenty of places to spend the day. Look for open movie theaters, cafés, and parks nearby, or join a community meal at a local center. You could also volunteer for an organization to meet people while contributing to a cause. Holiday hours vary, so it’s worth confirming before you head out.

    It has been revealed that if you’re single on Christmas, the day is yours to spend however you want. You could cook something you love, explore a latest spot, or go for a casual meal or movie with friends.

    It has been revealed that if you’re feeling sad or lonely on Christmas, let yourself feel those emotions without judgment. Consider reaching out to a loved one, even briefly. A short meditation can also bring some relief. If the sadness feels overwhelming or won’t lift, speak to a doctor or someone you trust.

    It’s okay to skip Christmas altogether. You can treat December 25 as an ordinary day: rest, work, or do something unrelated to the holiday. If the season stirs up grief or stress, stepping back from holiday plans is one way to look after yourself.

    According to recent reports, A solo tradition can be anything that brings you comfort, whether that’s a special breakfast, a journal entry, or a newly introduced ornament you pick out every year. A simple tradition is more likely to stick from year to year.

    Industry observers note that mental health is hard. Getting support doesn't have to be. The Calm app puts the tools to feel better in your back pocket, with personalized content to manage stress and anxiety, get better sleep, and feel more present in your life.
